activities.text: Ships were built at Aker Brygge until 1982, when the shipyard closed. The first buildings in the new neighborhood, with restaurants, stores, and homes, were completed in 1986. Follow the waterfront to Tjuvholmen, “Thieves’ Islet”: thieves were executed here in the 18th century. At its tip, a sculpture park designed by architect Renzo Piano sits beside a small swimming area. In summer, tuck a swimsuit into your bag.

visits.text: No foreign army has ever succeeded in taking Akershus Fortress (Akershus festning) by siege. Yet it surrendered without a fight in 1940: faced with the German invasion, the government had just evacuated the capital. King Haakon V had it built toward the end of the 1290s. After a fire in 1624, King Christian IV transformed it into a Renaissance castle. The fortress grounds along the fjord are free to explore. The castle (100 NOK, including an English audio guide) has opening hours that vary by season: check them before visiting.

visits.text: If you are traveling with children, set aside 1 hour 30 minutes for Akvariet i Bergen, the city’s aquarium. It opened in 1960 at the tip of the Nordnes peninsula. More than 300 species live here, from fish found along the Norwegian coast to crocodiles and snakes from tropical forests. The stars are still the penguins and sea lions, fed in front of visitors at scheduled times. The daily program, published on the aquarium’s website, lists feeding times. Adult admission: 380 kroner; a family ticket is available.

places.name: Alesund

visits.text: Ålesund's city centre is a unique case in Europe: on the night of 23 January 1904, a fire razed 850 houses in 16 hours and left 10,000 people homeless. The entire town was rebuilt in brick and concrete between 1904 and 1907 in the then-fashionable Art Nouveau style – hence this rare architectural coherence. Stroll along Kongens gate and St Olav square to see the turrets, ornate façades, and floral motifs.

The Jugendstilsenteret is housed in the former Svaneapoteket pharmacy from 1907, whose original interior has been preserved. The museum traces the 1904 fire, the accelerated reconstruction, and the Art Nouveau influences from Germany – Kaiser Wilhelm II, who regularly holidayed in Sunnmøre, had sent four relief ships after the disaster.

Ålesund's harbour and its quays facing the Sunnmøre Alps give the quintessential view of the town from the water. Walk to the end of Molovegen to see the old wooden warehouses - some converted into cafés - and the red lighthouse at the harbour entrance.

The Sunnmøre Museum, in Ålesund's Borgundgavlen district, displays historic houses and traditional boats that illustrate life on the coast. Explore the buildings of the open-air museum, then the exhibitions devoted to navigation and fishing to discover Sunnmøre's maritime heritage.

Atlanterhavsparken, on the Tueneset coast in Ålesund, presents the marine life of the Norwegian coast in its aquariums. Observe the cold-water fish, then head outside to the outdoor pools to see the seals and penguins.

activities.text: Climb the 418 steps to the Aksla viewpoint in Byparken park. The view over Ålesund and its islands, with the Sunnmøre Alps as backdrop, is the finest in town. The step numbers are printed on the risers if you need to keep count.

Walk along the Tueneset coast in Ålesund, near Atlanterhavsparken. Follow the coastal paths to see the rocks, small coves, and islands at the entrance to the fjord. Stop in the designated areas to watch the sea and the boats passing offshore, then return along the same path.

visits.text: All graves are anonymous at Tjøtta internasjonale krigskirkegård, the Tjøtta International War Cemetery, established in 1970. Those buried here include victims of the Rigel, a cargo ship requisitioned by the German army. On November 27, 1944, British aircraft bombed it, believing they were targeting German soldiers. Most of those aboard were Russian, Serbian, and Polish prisoners of war. More than 2,500 people died. The cemetery, between Tjøtta and Sandnessjøen, has a rest area with parking.

Although designed primarily for Norwegian visitors, the Petter Dass-museet is worth a stop, at least for its building, designed by the architecture firm Snøhetta and opened in 2007. Petter Dass was the pastor of Alstahaug from 1689 until his death in 1707. The poet described northern Norway in verse in The Trumpet of Nordland. For a hundred years after his death, many fishing boats in the north carried a black cloth in their sails as a sign of mourning. The museum is closed on Mondays.

Alstahaug kirke, next to the museum, is one of seven medieval churches still standing in northern Norway. It was completed around 1150, partly using locally sourced soapstone, a soft rock that is easy to carve. The small onion dome above the roof dates from a later restoration. The site's historic buildings, including the parsonage from the mid-18th century, are open from June through August, or by appointment.

visits.text: Hjemmeluft is the main area open to visitors within the Rock Art of Alta, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985. More than 6,000 carvings have been recorded in the Alta region, including around 3,000 at Hjemmeluft. Created over several millennia, they depict moose, reindeer, boats and hunting scenes among other subjects. Walkways allow visitors to explore the carvings while protecting the site.

The Alta Museum, located on the rock carving site since 1991, presents carving techniques, the life of Arctic hunter-gatherers, and the northern lights—the first permanent aurora observatory was built in Alta in the late 19th century.

Alta's Nordlyskatedralen (Northern Lights Cathedral), inaugurated in 2013, stands out for its titanium spiral rising toward the sky. It evokes an aurora frozen in architecture—the visit is brief but the exterior is worth the detour.

The Alta River is one of the world's most coveted salmon rivers—Atlantic salmon regularly exceed 25 kg here, and fishing rights for non-residents reach the equivalent of 30,000 NOK for three days. Each year, a lottery allocates 70 fishing days to visiting anglers from among 1,200 applicants. Even without a fishing rod, walking along the banks under the midnight sun is breathtaking.

The Sami Siida, just outside Alta, is a traditional Sami camp where you can feed reindeer, listen to stories around the fire, and taste bidos—Sami reindeer stew—in a real lavvu. It's one of the most accessible Sami cultural experiences from Alta.

In Alta, discover Sami and Kven cultures in the exhibitions at Alta Museum, on the Hjemmeluft site. The objects and stories on display introduce the region's traditions, activities and history. Explore the galleries devoted to local communities to understand how these cultures meet in Finnmark.

The return to Alta through Finnmark's interior takes you through landscapes of tundra, rivers, and dwarf birch forests—the vast, inhabited emptiness at the end of the world. In autumn, the ochre and golden colors of the tundra are spectacular.

activities.text: Sautso Canyon, on the Alta River, is the deepest canyon in Northern Europe, with walls reaching 400 m in height over a length of 22 km. Boat excursions let you travel alongside its cliffs - check local departures from Alta.

In winter, go dog sledding on Finnmarksvidda - Norway's largest plateau stretches as far as the eye can see. Local sled dog kennels offer 2 to 3-hour outings with their huskies. In summer, guided hikes with the dogs are also organised.

Alta is one of the world's northern lights capitals in winter—the surrounding countryside, far from city lights, offers a perfectly dark sky. The best nights are from September to March, between 6pm and 2am.

The Alta River is renowned for world-class salmon fishing—local guides organize outings on the water in summer, fly-fishing or spinning. In summer, you can also rent a canoe to paddle along the riverbanks at your own pace.

visits.text: Gudbrandsjuvet, along the National Scenic Route, is a narrow gorge with steel walkways suspended above waterfalls. Allow for a round trip during the day from Åndalsnes. Stop for 20 minutes - the viewpoint architecture is exemplary, and the site empties out quickly.

Trollstigen - literally “the Troll Ladder” - climbs through 11 hairpin bends on a 9% gradient to an elevation of 858 meters, with the Stigfossen waterfall (a 320 m drop) right beside the road. Opened on July 31, 1936, by King Haakon VII after 8 years of construction by hand, each bend bears the name of the foreman who built it. Allow for a round trip during the day from Åndalsnes.

From the panoramic platform at the top of Trollstigen, designed by Reiulf Ramstad Architects, you look down at the hairpin bends and see the Isterdalen valley opening toward the Atlantic. Allow for a round trip during the day from Åndalsnes. Allow 30 minutes up there - the visitor center's café is worth a stop.

Åndalsnes, Norway's mountaineering capital, nestles at the head of the Romsdalsfjord beneath Romsdalshorn (1,550 m). It is an ideal base for hikers - the Norsk Tindesenter on the harbor houses the mountaineering museum and an indoor climbing wall.

Trollveggen is Europe's highest vertical rock face - 1,100 metres of gneiss from the valley floor to the summit, with a 50-metre overhang at the top. You can see it from the E136, 10 km from Åndalsnes. The first ascents didn't happen until 1965 - a British amateur team, mocked by experts, had taken up the challenge.

Trollveggen visitor centre, at the foot of the wall on the E136, offers a panoramic terrace and a film on the history of climbing attempts and BASE jumping - banned since 1986 after several fatal accidents.

activities.text: Driving the Geiranger-Trollstigen tourist route (around 104 km). Trollstigen is closed from November to mid-May depending on snow conditions – check vegvesen.no before departure. Vehicles over 12.4 metres are prohibited.

Hike to Rampestreken from Åndalsnes – a cantilevered steel platform 550 metres above Romsdalsfjord. Allow 2 hours 30 minutes for the 4 km round trip. The ascent is steep but the trail is marked. The view over the valley and fjords is worth every metre of elevation gain.

visits.text: Stop by the Whale Center, the safari visitor center at Andenes harbor, before boarding. Its whale exhibition is included with every Whalesafari Andenes ticket. It introduces the species living offshore and the ocean conditions around the island. A one-hour guided tour is available for an additional 150 Norwegian kroner. A large center devoted to whales, The Whale, will also open in Andenes starting June 4, 2027. Arrive early: safari check-in takes place at the Whale Center.

Bright red against the pale sky, Andenes Lighthouse (Andenes fyr) rises 40 m above the northern tip of Andøya. Its cast-iron tower was assembled on-site from plates in the mid-19th century. Right next door, Andøymuseet tells the story of Hilmar Nøis, a trapper, or fur hunter. He spent 38 winters on Spitsbergen, the main island of the Svalbard archipelago. In summer, the museum offers guided climbs to the top of the lighthouse: 148 steps. Ask at the front desk for times.

Andenes’s most unexpected detour leads toward space. Andøya Space is Norway’s only active space center: research rockets have launched here since 1962. Its visitor center, Spaceship Aurora, explains the northern lights through an exhibition and a film. The virtual role-playing game Journey to Mars lets you spend 70 minutes in teams of six playing researchers sent to find out whether life exists on Mars. It is recommended for ages 10 and up. The center is open from May through late September: book online in summer.

activities.text: If you take just one boat trip, make it a whale-watching safari from Andenes. Very close to shore, the seabed plunges abruptly into an underwater canyon, Bleiksdjupet. The cold water rising from this canyon is rich in food. Male sperm whales live here year-round, diving very deep to hunt squid. Females stay in warmer waters, such as those around the Azores. From May to September, Whalesafari Andenes runs trips lasting 3 to 4 hours aboard a traditional boat. If you see neither a whale nor a dolphin, you are offered another trip free of charge.

days_plan.itin_title: Vesterålen in 4 Days: Andenes Whales, Bleik, and Nyksund

visits.text: On the E16 between Gudvangen and Voss, the road crosses the spectacular Nærøydalen valley, enclosed by steep mountainsides and dotted with numerous waterfalls. The old Stalheimskleiva road, famous for its 13 very tight hairpin bends, bears witness to the former route through this impressive terrain. Take your time to enjoy the views over the valley before continuing towards Voss.

Upon arrival in Bergen, stroll the Hanseatic wharf of Bryggen, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979. In 1360, the Hanseatic League established its trading office here and controlled the dried fish trade for nearly 400 years - Bergen is the only non-League city whose original medieval structure still stands within the urban fabric. The current appearance dates from the reconstruction after the 1702 fire; 62 buildings survive.

Explore the alleys and warehouses behind the waterfront of Bryggen - the facade along the wharf is what everyone photographs, but the back of the rows of houses is far more interesting. You'll find craft galleries, jewellers' and potters' workshops set in spaces that haven't changed since the 18th century. In high season, arrive before 9am to have the alleys to yourself.

Fisketorget fish market is one of Norway's oldest open-air markets. You'll find fresh salmon, langoustines and halibut - plus stalls selling prepared dishes. The adjacent indoor market, open year-round, is the best option outside summer.

The Nordnes peninsula, at the western tip of Bergen's centre, offers a pleasant walk along the shore with views over Byfjord. The coastal park of Nordnesparken at the point is where Bergen locals come to swim in summer - the water is cold but the setting is beautiful.

Fantoft Stave Church, in Paradis south of Bergen, is a reconstruction. The original, a 12th-century stave church moved from Fortun in 1883, burned down in an arson attack in 1992. The identical reconstruction was completed in 1997. Visit the exterior and grounds - the carved doors with intertwined dragon motifs are particularly detailed.

The Milde Arboretum, in southern Bergen, is one of Norway's largest botanical gardens, with 50 hectares of rhododendron, conifer and coastal plant collections. The paths follow coves and mossy woodland - this is quiet Bergen, away from the tourist crowds, approximately 23 km from Bergen city centre, a 30-minute drive.

activities.text: Drive from Flåm to Bergen via the E16: allow 3 hours, including photo stops in the Nærøydalen valley. The section between Gudvangen and Voss is the most spectacular - do not rush through it.

Take the Fløibanen funicular from the city centre up to Mount Fløyen (320 m) - in service since 1918, 850 metres of track, 6 minutes uphill. The panoramic view over Bergen, its seven mountains and Byfjord is the city's essential postcard shot. At the summit, marked trails lead into the troll forest - allow 30 to 45 minutes for the loop around Lake Skomakerdiket. Book online to skip the queue in summer.

Walk through Milde's coastal woodland and rocky coves - the paths around the arboretum extend for several kilometres towards the fjord. The terrain is easy, ideal for a morning's walk in Norwegian nature without straying far from Bergen. From Bergen, allow approximately 23 km and a 30-minute drive to reach Milde.

visits.text: A 13th-century royal banquet hall nearly vanished in 1944: Håkonshallen, at the heart of Bergenhus Fortress. King Håkon Håkonsson had it built for his celebrations. In 1261, his son Magnus’s wedding brought 2,000 guests here. On April 20, 1944, a cargo ship loaded with explosives blew up in the nearby harbor. The blast damaged the hall, and its wooden roof burned. Following restoration, it reopened in 1961. Check the calendar: the hall is closed to visitors on days when official events take place.

Next, climb Rosenkrantz Tower (Rosenkrantztårnet), within the same fortress. Its oldest section is a royal tower from the 1270s. In the 1560s, Erik Rosenkrantz, the fortress governor, had Scottish stonemasons expand it. Each level served a purpose: dungeons at the bottom, the governor’s quarters above, and cannons at the very top. The tower opens daily at 10 a.m., except December 21–31. Adult admission: 170 Norwegian kroner; free for visitors under 18.

visits.text: In Norwegian, “bleik” means pale: the white sand of Bleikstranda gave the village its name. This beach, just north of the houses, is among Norway’s longest. Walk along it in the evening, when the midnight sun lights up the sand and the silhouette of Bleiksøya island. The water stays very cold, even in midsummer: swimming is for the brave.

Bleik’s biggest surprise lies beneath your feet. The northern part of the village is built on a gårdshaug, a mound formed by the remains of farms and waste accumulated in the same place over centuries. Here, these layers reach a thickness of 6 m, the greatest depth measured in Norway for this type of mound. The village had to rebuild after a violent storm destroyed much of it in 1925. A 30-minute walk to the harbor and its breakwater is enough to look around.

activities.text: Seen from the beach, Bleiksøya island looks like a cone sitting on the sea, about 160 m high. Its cliffs host around 80,000 pairs of Atlantic puffins, small seabirds with colorful bills, from mid-April to early August. The island is a nature reserve where landing is prohibited. The boat operated by Puffin Safari, based in Bleik, reaches the colony in ten minutes. A white-tailed eagle, a large sea eagle, can eat about two puffins a day here in summer. Prices start at 800 Norwegian kroner.

visits.text: The fast crossing from Svolvær (or Skutvik) to Bodø across the Vestfjorden is by passenger-only express boat. If you are travelling with a car, arrange its transport separately: it cannot be taken aboard this service. Settle on the upper deck if the weather allows: the view of the Lofoten Islands receding to the north is spectacular. Bodø is 33 km north of the Arctic Circle.

Bodø's waterfront was completely rebuilt after the Second World War bombings in May 1940, which destroyed 75% of the town. Today, the harbour looks out towards the offshore islands and the mountains of Salten. It is a lively town and a departure point for ferries to the Lofoten Islands.

The Norwegian Aviation Museum (Norsk Luftfartsmuseum) opened in 1994—the building itself, seen from the air, traces the shape of an airplane propeller over 10,000 m². Inside, you'll encounter civilian and military aircraft from World War II to the present day, including a replica of the American U2 spy plane shot down in 1960 as it headed toward Bodø from Pakistan. Don't miss the flight simulator.

Moskenes→Bodø ferry: booking in advance is essential in summer—without a reservation, the wait can exceed 6 hours at the Moskenes dock. The crossing across Vestfjord takes 3 hours 15 minutes to 3 hours 45 minutes and can be choppy. It's also on this route that you can spot sea eagles and, in season, whales.

From Bodø, head to Saltstraumen 30 km southeast. In this 150-meter-wide strait, 400 million cubic meters of water rush through every 6 hours when the tide reverses, reaching 22 knots (40 km/h) and forming whirlpools 10 meters in diameter and 5 meters deep. It's officially the world's strongest tidal current, a phenomenon 2,000 to 3,000 years old. The spectacle is even more intense two to three days before or after the full and new moon—check tide times before going.

activities.text: The Saltstraumen, 33 km from Bodø, is the world's strongest tidal current: every 6 hours, 400 million cubic meters of water flow through a 150-meter-wide strait at speeds up to 20 knots (37 km/h), creating whirlpools 10 meters in diameter. Check schedules online before heading out—the phenomenon is invisible at slack tide. The effect is strongest on the days of the full and new moons.

If you have energy, climb Mount Keiservarden from Bodø for a panoramic view over the city, the sea and the silhouettes of the Lofoten on the horizon. That evening in Bodø is also the time to arrange the next leg: the flight to Tromsø the following morning.

visits.text: Turquoise water with a strip of ice at the far end: this is Lake Bondhusvatnet, at the foot of Bondhusbreen Glacier. Its color comes from glacial flour, a very fine rock dust ground down by the glacier. It floats in the water and mainly reflects blue and green light. Over the past century, the glacier has retreated considerably and is now visible only at the end of the valley. It was in this valley that Queen Sonja of Norway officially opened Folgefonna National Park on May 14, 2005. Picnic tables await by the water.

If you follow the Maurangsfjord along the Fv551 near Sundal, Furebergsfossen waterfall flows beneath the road. After a free fall of 20 m, the water flows straight into this arm of the Hardangerfjord. You can get very close, and a rainbow often forms in the spray. Do not stop on the roadway: the road is narrow and hugs the cliff, so park in the small parking lot nearby.

activities.text: In 1863, shipowner Johan Martin Dahll had the Isvegen, the “ice road,” built to sell ice from Bondhusbreen Glacier. Blocks weighing about 18 kg crossed the lake by rowboat, then traveled down to the dock by cart. They were used to keep food cool before the invention of the refrigerator. Much of the ice melted during the journey, and the trade ended after a few shipments. Today, this 2.3 km gravel path leads to Lake Bondhusvatnet on foot: allow 2 hours round-trip for this easy walk.

visits.text: Briksdalsbreen now ends on dry land, behind its small glacial lake. Yet this arm of Jostedalsbreen made headlines in the 1990s. Between 1967 and 1997, it advanced 465 m and covered the entire lake, while most of Europe’s glaciers were retreating. Since then, it too has been retreating: by 2007, it no longer reached the lake. Keep your distance from the glacier’s edge, as blocks of ice can break off without warning.

activities.text: You will walk about 3 km, with 200 m of elevation gain, from the bottom of the Briksdal valley to the lake at Briksdalsbreen. About a third of the way along, spray from Kleivafossen waterfall drenches the trail: keep a windbreaker handy. Allow 2 hours 30 minutes to 3 hours for the round-trip walk. The troll cars, small electric carts that run from May through October, reduce the walk to 700 m. Leave Loen early: many excursions from cruise ships calling at Olden come up here.

visits.text: As early as around 1200, a church stood on the site of Brønnøy kirke in central Brønnøysund. The current cross-shaped building, made of brown stone, dates from 1870. It replaced the old church, which was damaged by fires in 1772 and 1866. Its oldest object is a wooden crucifix dating from before the Protestant Reformation. Allow 30 minutes: the church is a few minutes’ walk from the harbor.

Havnegata, Brønnøysund’s harbor street, is the best place to watch daily life in this town of about 5,000 residents. Small boats come and go between the islands. Every day, the Hurtigruten, the coastal express that travels along Norway’s coast, calls at the dock. Throughout the country, the town is best known for Brønnøysundregistrene, the agency that maintains Norway’s business register. Come in the afternoon, when the southbound Hurtigruten calls.

activities.text: The scent of herbs greets you at the entrance to Hildurs Urterarium, an herb garden in Tilrem, about 7 km from Brønnøysund. Hildur and her husband handed their farm over to the next generation in 1988. She then created this garden and its restaurant. The plants are grouped by theme: culinary herbs, medicinal plants, and heirloom varieties. The roughly 250-year-old farmhouse stands in the shade of a 150-year-old elm.

visits.text: The best of Bryggen lies behind the facades: leave the waterfront and follow the narrow wooden passageways between the houses. This merchants’ quarter, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979, retains around 62 wooden buildings. Their current appearance dates from the rebuilding that followed the fire of 1702. From 1350 onward, the Hanseatic League, an alliance of Northern European trading cities, maintained its trading office here. From October through December, a guided tour of Schøtstuene and Bryggen in English takes place on Saturdays and Sundays at noon.

visits.text: “Ást min, kyss mik,” meaning “my love, kiss me”: this medieval love note, carved in runes, is preserved at Bryggens Museum. Runes are the ancient alphabet of the Scandinavian peoples. The museum holds around 670 of these messages, most carved into pine wood and discovered in and around Bryggen since the fire of 1955. The museum building, dating from 1976, stands over the foundations of Bergen’s oldest houses, built in the first half of the 12th century. Open daily; free for visitors under 18.

activities.text: For a chance to get near a glacier without a guide, Buarbreen makes a rewarding half-day outing from Odda. This outlet of the vast Folgefonna Glacier descends into the Buer valley, which you can reach by car, about 8 km from town. The marked trail is moderately difficult and runs 3 km each way, with about 600 m of elevation gain: allow 4 hours round-trip. It follows the river and crosses it on footbridges. Fixed ropes help you climb in places, and the final section is steep. Wear proper hiking boots.

visits.text: According to legend, the statue of Saint Nicholas at Eidsborg stavkyrkje was immersed in a nearby pond every Midsummer Eve. This small medieval stave church stands in the hills above Dalen. Unusually, shingles—small wooden boards laid like tiles—cover both its walls and its roof. It is part of the Vest-Telemark Museum, an open-air museum that also preserves a wooden building dating to 1184. Admission: 150 NOK. The church opens only for guided tours at 11 a.m., 1 p.m., and 3 p.m., from mid-June to mid-August.

If you drop a banknote over the edge of Ravnejuvet, the “Raven’s Gorge,” it may float back up toward you, according to a story told in the valley. The explanation is simple: an updraft rises along the cliff face and pushes light objects upward. The cliff drops sheer for about 350 m to the Tokkeåi River. Access is via a narrow gravel road about 7 km long. Drive slowly, and approach the edge with caution.

activities.text: Start early to climb the 810 stone steps from Dalen to Rui, on the hillside above the village. Sherpas from Nepal built this staircase using local whetstone, a rock the region has exported for about a thousand years. Over 1 km, you gain 200 m in elevation, a climb of 20 to 30 minutes. The trail follows in the footsteps of two sisters from Rui, Ingerine and Gurine. Their life-size statues stand outside the Dalen tourist information office, which sells a book about their story.
