activities.text: According to legend, De syv søstre, the Seven Sisters, are troll sisters chased along the coast by another troll, the Horseman. The first rays of sunlight turned them to stone. The mountain range rises to 1,072 m east of Sandnessjøen. From the Markvoll parking lot, 4.7 km from Søvik, a marked 1.5 km trail climbs 250 m to Markvollkulpen, a series of natural pools and a small waterfall at the foot of Skjæringen and Tvillingan.

days_plan.itin_title: Helgeland Coast in 5 Days: Torghatten, Vega, and Svartisen

visits.text: The Jæren Scenic Route follows 70 km of flat, windswept coastline—a geographical curiosity in Norway, land of mountains. Wild sandy beaches, dunes, and lighthouses unfold along this route protected since 1977.

Obrestad lighthouse (Obrestad fyr), built from solid granite in 1873, is the first land-based lighthouse on the Jæren coast. In its basement, German soldiers left frescoes during the occupation - these are accessible to visitors. Plan this as a day trip by car from Egersund.
Painted wooden houses line the harbor in Egersund's historic town center—a preserved maritime atmosphere and a few waterfront cafes. Allow 45 minutes to explore at leisure.

activities.text: The beaches of Bore and Orrestranden are among Norway's most beautiful: Orrestranden stretches over 3 km of white sand, while Borestranden is the go-to surf spot in Jæren. Wind, waves and an unobstructed horizon over the North Sea - a complete change of scenery. Plan this as a day trip by car from Egersund.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Norway Road Trip: Stavanger, Preikestolen, Lysefjord & the South Coast

visits.text: If you visit in summer, step inside Kjeldsenbruket, the former fish processing plant beside the dock in Ekkerøy. It is one of the few plants of its kind in Finnmark to have survived World War II. In the fall of 1944, the Soviet army advanced so quickly that German soldiers had no time to burn the village. You can still see the dock, grocery store, and cooker used to extract cod liver oil. The café and exhibitions open only in summer.

activities.text: The cries of black-legged kittiwakes drown out the wind at the foot of Flåget, the cliff in Ekkerøy Nature Reserve. Tens of thousands of these small, black-legged gulls nest here. This may be Norway’s most easily accessible seabird cliff. The 6.1 km loop circles Ekkerøy, a former island connected to the mainland by an isthmus, a narrow strip of land. At the top, you pass Gerda and Paula, two German gun emplacements that guarded the entrance to the fjord. Allow 2 hours for the walk.

Next, turn off the E75 toward Komagvær, farther east, and follow 7 km of unpaved road to Komagdalen, the valley of the Komagelva River. From Ekkerøy, plan on a round trip by car within the day, including the unpaved section. The parking lot marks the boundary of Varangerhalvøya National Park, established in 2006. The park covers 1,804 km², mostly tundra, an almost treeless landscape of plateaus, boulders, and peat bogs. A bird trail starts at the parking lot, with information panels about species such as the long-tailed jaeger, a characteristic bird of the park. The unpaved road is rough: drive slowly, preferably in a vehicle with high ground clearance.

days_plan.itin_title: Varanger in 4 Days: Kirkenes, Vardø, and Hamningberg

visits.text: Between 1999 and 2022, the Engabreen glacier front retreated approximately 700 m, according to the Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate (NVE). Engabreen is a tongue of the Svartisen glacier—an arm of ice descending from the plateau. It once reached almost all the way to the fjord. Today, it ends at an elevation of around 110 m, above Lake Engabrevatnet. Beneath the ice, a laboratory allows researchers to observe the glacier bed under nearly 200 m of ice. Stay at the cairn, the pile of stones marking the end of the trail: blocks of ice can fall without warning.

activities.text: You will cross Holandsfjorden in 15 minutes aboard Isprins, the shuttle departing from Holandsvika. From the dock at Engen, a gravel track follows Lake Engabrevatnet for 3 km. A rocky trail then leads to the cairn, 4.3 km from the dock. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours each way, with approximately 190 m of elevation gain. The last 500 meters are the steepest.

Svartisgryta, approximately 600 m beyond the cairn, is a glacial pothole: a large, round hollow carved into the rock by ice and water. In warm weather, some hikers swim in it. The detour follows a marked trail and adds 30 minutes to the walk to Engabreen.

If the wind picks up, Brestua, the summer café on the shore of Lake Engabrevatnet, offers a break with views of Engabreen. It is a 15- or 20-minute walk from the dock at Engen, near the start of the hike. It is a good place to warm up on your return from the glacier. This café is open only in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Helgeland Coast in 5 Days: Torghatten, Vega, and Svartisen

activities.text: Pick up your rental car at Harstad/Narvik Airport, Evenes, the starting point for this itinerary through Vesterålen. Allow about 1 hour 40 minutes for the 121 km drive to Sortland. The E10 first crosses the Tjeldsund Bridge, then you head toward Gullesfjord. The Rv85 then takes you north to the blue town. In summer, the sun barely sets at these latitudes: even an evening arrival leaves enough daylight to enjoy the drive.

days_plan.itin_title: Vesterålen in 4 Days: Andenes Whales, Bleik, and Nyksund

visits.text: Norwegians call their traditional festive costume a “bunad.” The national institute devoted to these costumes is housed at Valdres Folkemuseum, the open-air museum in Fagernes. Founded in 1901, the museum brings together more than 100 historic buildings and structures on a peninsula in Lake Strondafjorden, 800 m from the center. Pigs, chickens, and sheep roam between the farms. Allow 2 hours. In midsummer, the museum is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and an adult ticket costs 140 NOK.

activities.text: You will end the day on Vesleøya, an uninhabited islet connected to the shore in Fagernes by a small white wooden footbridge. It lies about 50 m from the shore of Lake Strondafjorden. It makes for a short, peaceful evening walk, just a few minutes on foot from the center.

days_plan.itin_title: Norway’s Mountains in 5 Days: Lillehammer and Jotunheimen

activities.text: The most scenic way to reach Femundsmarka is still aboard Fæmund II, a metal-hulled boat that has sailed Lake Femund since 1905. Too large to be transported in one piece, it arrived in sections at Synnervika, where it was assembled. Its boiler, the heart of the steam engine, was too large to be cut apart: six horses pulled it on a sled. Femund, Norway’s third-largest lake, stretches for 60 km at an elevation of 662 m. In summer, the boat leaves Synnervika daily at 9 a.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Røros in 3 Days: Copper Town, Mine, and Lake Femund

visits.text: Røvollen is a self-service cabin with no warden, run by the Norwegian Trekking Association (DNT). It occupies a former summer pasture, a meadow where livestock were taken in summer. These meadows attracted unexpected visitors: musk oxen. A small herd from the Dovrefjell mountains settled in the area in 1971. The animals came here to graze. By 2021, only seven animals remained in the herd. If you encounter any, back away calmly and stay at least 200 m away.

Here, even dead trees are protected. Femundsmarka National Park, established in 1971, stretches between Lake Femund and the Swedish border. Its old, dead pines support rare species, including a lichen called ulvelav. The landscape of scattered pines, boulders, and lakes has changed little since the ice retreated about 10,000 years ago. The Sámi, the Indigenous people of northern Scandinavia, have herded their reindeer here since the 17th century. Campfires are prohibited from April 15 to September 15.

activities.text: Get off the Fæmund II at the Røa dock, in the busiest area of Femundsmarka National Park. A trail marked with the letter T leads to Røvollen cabin in an hour to an hour and a half. The cabin is near the Røa River, which flows down from Sweden to Lake Femund. Have a picnic there, then head back to the dock without lingering. The boat passes only once a day in each direction: note the return time on the timetable before getting off.

days_plan.itin_title: Røros in 3 Days: Copper Town, Mine, and Lake Femund

activities.text: The smell of the sea and the calls of fishmongers: Fisketorget, Bergen’s fish market, is a good place to start the day. Merchants and fishermen have gathered here since the 1200s. Since 2012, an indoor market hall, Mathallen, has brought together fishmongers and restaurants year-round. The outdoor stalls only open from May through the end of summer. Prices are high: ask for the price per kilogram before ordering.

days_plan.itin_title: Bergen in 2 Days: Bryggen, Fløyen, Ulriken, and Grieg

visits.text: Even in perfect weather, start at Norsk Bremuseum, the Norwegian Glacier Museum: it explains everything you will see afterward. The concrete and wood building was designed by Sverre Fehn, who won the Pritzker Prize, a major international architecture award, in 1997. You can handle ice taken from Supphellebreen, a nearby glacier. A film on a panoramic screen takes you into Jostedalsbreen National Park. The museum opens daily from April through October, with hours of 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. in June, July, and August; admission is 180 NOK.

Less than five minutes by car from the museum, a startling sight awaits: Bøyabreen, an arm of Jostedalsbreen, has melted so much in recent years that only remnants of ice remain. At its foot, the small lake Brevatnet collects meltwater. Waterfalls tumble down the cliffs at the head of the valley. Here you can see firsthand the glacial retreat the museum has just explained. Park in the nearest parking lot: a 200 m walk leads to the shore. A café and restaurant that opened in 1960 faces the glacier.

In Norwegian, it is called Bokbyen, “the book town.” In Fjærland, about 4 km of shelves filled with used books occupy the old buildings of the hamlet of Mundal. Browse the shelves in a former ferry waiting room, a barn, a bank, or a post office. Established in 1996, it was the first book town in the Nordic countries. The shops open daily from May through September, except on May 17, Norway’s national day.

The white wooden Fjærland Church has stood beside the fjord since 1861. It was once called Mundal Church, after the neighboring hamlet. In Norway, family names often come from the family’s original farm. This is how Walter Mondale, vice president of the United States from 1977 to 1981, got his name from this hamlet, where his paternal grandparents were born. The church is just steps from the bookstores: visit both on foot.

days_plan.itin_title: Jostedalsbreen in 4 Days: Urnes, Fjærland, and Loen

visits.text: Leaving Oslo on the E16, stop at Sundvollen for views over Tyrifjorden - one of Norway's largest lakes, nestled between conifer forests and hills. Continue on the E16 towards Fagernes and Lærdal, through valleys, forests and mountain landscapes dotted with red wooden farm buildings.

On the E16 between Lærdal and Aurland, you enter the Lærdal Tunnel - 24.5 km long, making it the world's longest road tunnel, opened in 2000. To break the monotony, engineers carved out three large caverns lit in blue and yellow at regular intervals. Don't speed: the limit is 80 km/h.

If the road is open, you can replace the drive through the Lærdal Tunnel with the scenic Aurlandsfjellet road (FV243), which crosses the mountains between Lærdal and Aurland. It offers high-mountain scenery and spectacular views down over the Aurlandsfjord. Allow more time than for the tunnel route. The section crossing the mountain plateau is closed in winter.

The Flåmsbana Museum, with free admission beside the station, traces the 20 years of construction of the Flåm Railway (1923–1940). The 20 km line descends 866 metres between Myrdal and Flåm, with a maximum gradient of 5.5% - one of the steepest in the world for standard gauge. 18 of the 20 tunnels were dug by hand by teams of 120 to 220 workers.

Otternes Bygdetun is a historic farm hamlet overlooking the Aurlandsfjord, about 4 km from Flåm. Its collection of wooden buildings reflects several centuries of traditional farming life in the region. The site can be reached by car or on foot from Flåm along the fjord. From the hamlet's meadows, there are beautiful views over the Aurlandsfjord and surrounding mountains.

Aurlandsvangen, the main village of the municipality of Aurland, 7 km from Flåm, has a peaceful waterfront on the Aurlandsfjord. Stop here in the late afternoon to see the evening light on the fjord's calm waters.

From the electric boat, the walls of the Nærøyfjord rise to 1,800 metres - and the fjord is only 250 metres wide at its narrowest point. The fjord has been UNESCO-listed since 2005: you will pass farms accessible only by boat. Book your tickets ahead in summer - the boats sail full.

Gudvangen, at the terminus of Nærøyfjord, is a village of a few dozen inhabitants squeezed between vertiginous cliffs. Its name means 'field of the gods at the water's edge' in Old Norse. Stop to see Kjelfossen waterfall, which plunges more than 800 metres from the heights.

activities.text: Drive from Oslo to Flåm via the E16. The road is passable all year round, but winter conditions can occur from November to April. Check vegvesen.no for road conditions before setting off.

Hike or photo walk along Flåm harbour and the shore of Aurlandsfjord. The village is tiny - a few hundred inhabitants - but the setting between fjord and sheer mountains is arresting. In high season, dozens of cruise ships anchor in the bay: arrive early in the morning for peace and quiet.

Silent cruise by electric boat on Nærøyfjord between Flåm and Gudvangen - 2 hours one way. The boat “Future of the Fjords”, fully electric since 2018, glides soundlessly between the fjord walls. The absence of an internal combustion engine is striking: you hear only waterfalls and the cries of eagles. Several departures daily, year-round.

days_plan.itin_title: Norway Road Trip: Oslo, Fjords & Bergen
Norway Road Trip: Oslo, Fjords & Bergen
Norway Road Trip: Oslo, Fjords & Bergen

visits.text: The best panoramic view of Bergen is from the terrace on Fløyen, 320 m above sea level. You can take in the city, the fjord, and the surrounding mountains at a glance. The name Fløyen may come from a weather vane that once showed sailing ships the wind direction. In winter, night falls early, but the paths leading back down to the city are lit. The illuminated city can then be seen from afar. The summit restaurant, Fløirestauranten, opens daily.

activities.text: If you visit in summer, buy your Fløibanen ticket online or in the app: it costs less than at the ticket counter. This funicular, in service since 1918, climbs 302 m in about six minutes. Along its 848 m track, the incline reaches 26 degrees. The lower station is a five-minute walk from the fish market. You cannot reserve a departure time: when it is busy, departures run one after another.

Then follow the path to Lake Skomakerdiket, about a ten-minute walk from Fløyen’s upper station. In summer, canoes are available to borrow for free. Goats also graze on the mountain during this season. With children, stop by Trollskogen, the “troll forest,” and the large playground. To get back down, allow about 45 minutes to walk to the city center, or take the funicular again.

days_plan.itin_title: Bergen in 2 Days: Bryggen, Fløyen, Ulriken, and Grieg

visits.text: You can board the Fram, the polar ship on display at the Frammuseet. Its rounded hull was designed so that closing ice would lift the ship instead of crushing it. This allowed explorer Fridtjof Nansen to leave it trapped in the Arctic pack ice for nearly three years. Roald Amundsen later sailed it toward Antarctica for his 1910 to 1912 expedition, the first to reach the South Pole. Walk around the hull before heading up on deck. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.; admission is 180 NOK.

days_plan.itin_title: Oslo in 2 Days: MUNCH, Vigeland, the Opera House, and Bygdøy

visits.text: Few fortified towns are as easy to explore as Gamlebyen, Fredrikstad’s old town. King Frederik II founded it in 1567 to replace Sarpsborg, the neighboring town burned down by the Swedish army. His statue stands in Kongens torv, the King’s Square. To the southeast, facing the Glomma River, the Provianthuset, a former army provisions storehouse built in 1674, is the district’s oldest surviving building. Shops and artists’ studios are open year-round, even on Sundays.

Beneath your feet, the grassy ramparts form a star around Gamlebyen. This shape follows the Dutch system of bastions, pointed projections from which defenders could fire along the walls. Willem Coucheron drew up the plans, and construction began in 1663. The moats are more than 40 m wide in places. They are shallow, but a deeper channel runs down the middle to prevent enemies from wading across. You can walk around the ramparts freely, day or night.

Gamlebyen’s largest building was once a military equipment warehouse: the Tøihuset, built in 1775, now houses the Fredrikstad Museum. On the ground floor, “Bar 1567” presents the city’s history interactively, as though a bartender were telling it to customers. Upstairs, a timeline connects the objects on display with the stories of local residents. An exhibition covering more than 500 m² traces the German invasion of Østfold in April 1940 and the local resistance. Admission costs 120 Norwegian kroner (NOK) per adult.

To see Gamlebyen from above, walk to Kongsten Fort, about 500 m east of the old town. It was built around 1680 on Galgeberget, “Gallows Hill.” The fort prevented enemies from occupying this high ground, where their cannons would have commanded the town and had a longer range. Today, the view stretches across Fredrikstad and the surrounding countryside. Head up late in the day, after visiting the museums.

Fredrikstad domkirke, a red-brick cathedral, stands in the modern city center on the west bank of the Glomma River. It was consecrated in 1880 and built in a Gothic Revival style modeled on medieval churches. Its spire rises to 72 m. In the chancel, Emanuel Vigeland’s stained-glass windows date from 1917 and depict angels playing music and the parable of the prodigal son. The church was only named a cathedral in 1969. Stop by just after taking the ferry across from Gamlebyen.

Long before Gamlebyen, there was Isegran, a small green island in the middle of the Glomma River. It is the first place in Fredrikstad mentioned in the archives: in the late 13th century, Count Alv Erlingsson maintained a small fortress here. Until 1680, the island was Norway’s only naval port. Wooden boats are restored here today, and the island is home to the country’s only school of traditional boatbuilding. Reach it on foot via the Kråkerøy Bridge or take the city ferry.

activities.text: The shortest crossing of the trip is also one of the most enjoyable: the Gamlebyfergen connects Cicignon, on the west bank of the Glomma River, to Gamlebyen in about one minute. This city ferry is free, including for bicycles. Fredrikstad municipality introduced its first motorized ferries in the early 1930s. Each boat carries a maximum of 50 passengers. On busy days, a full ferry may therefore pass the dock without stopping.

You can also spend longer on the water. Another free municipal ferry travels down the Glomma River from Gamlebyen to Ålekilen in about 22 minutes. It stops at Smertu, the city center, Værste, and Gressvik. This lets you watch both banks of Fredrikstad drift by without paying for a ticket. For the return trip, you must get off at the last stop and line up again.

days_plan.itin_title: Østfold in 3 Days: Fredrikstad, Halden, and the Hvaler Islands

activities.text: Pick up your rental car at Oslo Gardermoen Airport, about 47 km north of downtown Oslo. This route skips the capital and heads straight for the mountains. Lillehammer is 145 km north along the E6, a drive of less than 2 hours. If you land in the afternoon, save Maihaugen for the following morning: in summer, the museum generally opens at 10 a.m.

Long before airplanes, Gardermoen was a Norwegian army camp, dating back to 1740. The first flight took place here in 1912. The site became Oslo’s main airport on October 8, 1998, when the old Fornebu Airport closed. From Fagernes, allow for about 165 km and a little over two hours of driving. Leave extra time to refuel and return your rental car.

days_plan.itin_title: Norway’s Mountains in 5 Days: Lillehammer and Jotunheimen
Norway’s Mountains in 5 Days: Lillehammer and Jotunheimen

visits.text: On a clear day, Gaustatoppen (1,883 m) offers views of nearly one-sixth of mainland Norway, an area of about 60,000 km². Gaustatoppen turisthytte, a staffed mountain lodge built in 1893 from stone from the mountain, serves drinks and simple meals from February to mid-October. From the lodge, allow about 20 minutes to walk over rocky terrain to the highest point. Even in July, bring a warm jacket and closed-toe shoes: at this elevation, it is considerably cooler than in Rjukan.

activities.text: Ascend Gaustatoppen through the mountain aboard Gaustabanen, the underground train. The first car travels horizontally through an 850 m tunnel. A second then climbs a very steep passage at a 39-degree incline to an elevation of 1,800 m. The Norwegian military and NATO had the tunnel excavated in the 1950s to provide year-round access to a military radio station at the summit. It has been open to the public since 2004. The ride takes about 15 minutes. Round-trip tickets cost 595 NOK per adult and 300 NOK for ages 5 to 15.

days_plan.itin_title: Telemark in 4 Days: Rjukan, Heddal, and the Telemark Canal

visits.text: Flydalsjuvet viewpoint, accessible by car from Geiranger, offers the postcard view with the fjord below and the tiny village of Geiranger in the distance. This is where most aerial photos of the fjord are taken – go early in the morning to avoid the coaches.

Ørnesvingen (the Eagle's Bend), on the tourist route descending towards Geiranger, offers a direct panorama of the Seven Sisters and the fjord from the clifftop. On clear days, you can see the green water 600 metres below.

The Norwegian Fjord Centre (Norsk Fjordsenter) traces the history of inhabitants who lived on the farms overlooking Geirangerfjord. The fjord has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005 - both for its landscapes and for the traces of agricultural life in extreme conditions.

Dalsnibba (1,476 m) is Europe's highest viewpoint above a fjord accessible by car, about half an hour's drive from Geiranger. The toll road winds up from Geiranger - below, you can see cruise ships that look like toys. The cantilevered Skywalk extends over the drop above the fjord.

activities.text: Hellesylt-Geiranger cruise through UNESCO-listed Geirangerfjord. The Seven Sisters (De sju systre) cascade 410 metres in seven parallel streams down the fjord's north wall – opposite, the Suitor (Friaren) answers them from the other shore according to local legend. The journey takes around 1 hour 30 minutes depending on conditions.

Hike to the abandoned Skageflå farm, perched 250 metres above the fjord. Take the cruise out from Geiranger to be dropped off at the foot of the cliff, then climb the steep trail to the empty farm buildings. The view of the Seven Sisters from the same level offers a new perspective.

Kayak on Geirangerfjord at the foot of the waterfalls - the silence between the 1,700-metre walls is striking. Set out early morning when the cruise ships haven't yet arrived. Rental companies offer equipment and guides from Geiranger harbour.

days_plan.itin_title: Central Norway Road Trip: Ålesund, Geirangerfjord, Trollstigen & Trondheim
Central Norway Road Trip: Ålesund, Geirangerfjord, Trollstigen & Trondheim

activities.text: The water of Lake Gjende is a milky green. This color comes from rock flour: a very fine powder ground by glaciers and carried into the lake by the Muru River. From Gjendesheim, at the eastern end of the lake, the boat takes you to Memurubu, the starting point for Besseggen. A one-way ticket costs 260 NOK per adult. Buy your ticket online and take a screenshot, as cell phone reception is poor in places.

You will hike back from Memurubu to Gjendesheim along the Besseggen ridge: about 14 km, nearly 1,000 m of ascent, and 6 to 8 hours including breaks. On the ridge, you walk between two lakes: green Gjende and blue Bessvatnet, perched nearly 400 m higher. The highest point, Veslfjellet, reaches 1,743 m. In Henrik Ibsen’s play Peer Gynt, the hero tells of crossing this ridge on the back of a reindeer. Bring at least one liter of water, a windbreaker, and a map.

days_plan.itin_title: Norway’s Mountains in 5 Days: Lillehammer and Jotunheimen

visits.text: Grønsvik kystfort, a coastal fort beside Fv17, was part of the Atlantic Wall. This chain of German fortifications stretched from the French-Spanish border to northern Norway. The occupying forces made 77 Soviet prisoners and 65 Polish prisoners build it. They excavated rooms and tunnels in the rock. Seven Soviet prisoners died during construction; their remains are buried in Tjøtta Cemetery. The fort is 2 km north of the Stokkvågen junction.

activities.text: If you stay on the ferry's deck between Kilboghamn and Jektvik, you will cross the Arctic Circle. A globe on the small islet of Vikingen marks this line. It is illuminated at night and serves as a landmark for sailors. The Arctic Circle is the theoretical boundary beyond which the midnight sun can be seen. The crew generally announces the crossing during the trip, which takes a little over an hour.

days_plan.itin_title: Helgeland Coast in 5 Days: Torghatten, Vega, and Svartisen

visits.text: From the top of Fredriksten’s walls, the view stretches across Halden, the fjord, and the lands of its former Swedish enemy. Construction of the fortress began in 1661, after the loss of the neighboring province of Bohuslän, ceded to Sweden in 1658. It withstood six attacks without ever being captured. Its walls cover about 20,000 m², and three separate forts protect it. The grounds remain open day and night, and admission is free.

On December 11, 1718, King Charles XII of Sweden was killed outside Fredriksten. Fredriksten Museum tells the story of his death and Halden’s military history, from the 1640s to 1905. It occupies the Østre kurtine, the eastern curtain wall: the long wall connecting two bastions. The exhibition “Det store fallet” (“The Great Fall”) covers everything from the king’s underwear to the monuments erected after his death. On the top floor, the former water tower offers panoramic views. The museum opens only during the warmer months: after mid-August, it is open only on weekends, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

To save their town, the people of Halden burned it down. On July 4, 1716, Charles XII’s troops attacked at night. The residents then set fire to their own homes to keep the enemy from using them. The fortress held firm. Today, south of the pedestrian street, the Sørhalden neighborhood retains beautiful Empire-style houses, reflecting the neoclassicism of the early 19th century. Finish with a walk along the Tista, the river that runs through Halden.

If you have an extra morning in Halden, save it for Rød herregård, one of Norway’s best-preserved manor houses. Its garden, originally Baroque, was later expanded into an English landscape park. A curiosity lies hidden there. Ships delivering Norwegian timber to England returned loaded with English soil, used as ballast to stabilize them. Seeds in that soil gave rise to plants that still leave their mark on the garden. Guided tours of the house are available from May to September.

activities.text: Follow Karl XIIs sti, the Charles XII trail, from Halden’s market square to the fortress. The walk takes about 30 minutes. At each stop, the free Kulturpunkt app gives voice to a figure from the period, who describes their connection to the king. The trail ends at the Stevnesletta monument, erected in 1938 by Norway and Sweden near the spot where Charles XII fell. The king was standing in a trench about 170 m from the fortress. It is still uncertain who fired the shot.

days_plan.itin_title: Østfold in 3 Days: Fredrikstad, Halden, and the Hvaler Islands

visits.text: One of the best roadside views of Svartisen is from the Braset picnic area, just south of Holandsvika. Svartisen is Norway's second-largest glacier. Its name comes from svart, “black,” and is, “ice”: the old ice here looks darker than fresh snow. Stop on your way to catch the boat from Holandsvika, camera in hand.

activities.text: You will stay overnight in Halsa, a village in Meløy along Fv17, just after the ten-minute ferry crossing of the fjord from Ågskardet. Halsa is the most convenient base for Engabreen. Boats to the glacier leave from Holandsvika, about ten kilometers away. In summer, the first boat leaves at 10 a.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Helgeland Coast in 5 Days: Torghatten, Vega, and Svartisen

visits.text: The Struve Meridian Column at Fuglenes (UNESCO since 2005) is the northernmost point of a network of 265 triangulation stations stretching from Norway to the Black Sea—a 19th-century scientific project to measure the exact shape of the Earth. The walk to the monument offers a fine view over the harbor.

The Gjenreisningsmuseet tells how retreating Nazi forces razed Hammerfest in 1944—only the cemetery chapel remained standing. Audio testimonies from survivors, photographs, and period interior reconstructions show what it meant to rebuild everything from scratch. Allow at least an hour.
Hammerfest Church, rebuilt in 1961, has a triangular form inspired by traditional Sami tents—a subtle echo of the region's Sami past in a resolutely modern building.

The Isbjørnklubben (Royal Polar Bear Club) is a local institution founded in 1963—you can become a member by signing the register, which earns you a stamped diploma. A local curiosity worth seeing if you're passing through.

activities.text: Stroll along Hammerfest's waterfront: the harbor is lively, the multicolored 1950s houses tell the story of reconstruction, and you can watch seabirds from the pier in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Norway Road Trip: Tromsø, Alta & North Cape

visits.text: Abandoned, but not in ruins: Hamningberg is one of the few villages in Finnmark that the German army did not burn during its retreat in late 1944. About 65 old buildings are still standing: houses, boathouses, and warehouses. The fishermen sold their catch to the Pomors, Russian merchants. Many of the log houses were actually built in Russia and then reassembled here. In 1940, 700 people lived here. The village emptied out in the 1960s because its harbor offered too little shelter for modern boats. Walk past the wooden chapel built in 1949, which is protected as a historic landmark.

In May and early summer, Hamningberg’s birdwatching shelter lets you watch the sea out of the wind. It was designed by the architecture firm Biotope. Seabirds pass offshore. You can sometimes spot porpoises and minke whales, a species of whale, and, more rarely, orcas. To the west, the cliff of Syltefjordstauran is home to a large colony of northern gannets, large seabirds. Bring binoculars and a warm layer: it is easy to spend an hour standing still.

activities.text: You follow the final stretch of the Varanger National Scenic Route, which runs 160 km from Varangerbotn. After Vardø, the road to Hamningberg becomes narrow and winding. Along the coast, the weathered rocks often evoke a lunar landscape. Near Persfjorden, waves and frost have sculpted rocky spires that resemble trolls. Some of these rocks are more than 500 million years old. Stop at roadside pullouts for photos, and watch for reindeer.

If the weather is clear, climb Hardbaken, the hill that shelters Hamningberg from the north wind. A path leads from the village to the remains of a German coastal fort from World War II. From the top, the view takes in the Barents Sea and the rugged coastline. Look for snow buntings, small birds often seen on these heights. The paths are not maintained: follow the existing tracks, as the ground is slippery when wet.

days_plan.itin_title: Varanger in 4 Days: Kirkenes, Vardø, and Hamningberg

visits.text: The most beautiful landmark of the trip comes at the very first stop: Heddal stavkirke, or Heddal Stave Church. “Stave” means its walls are supported by large vertical wooden posts rather than horizontal logs. It dates from the 13th century. Standing 29 m tall, it is the largest church of its kind in Norway. Inside, look for the 23 masks carved on the pillars. The adult ticket (110 NOK) includes a guided tour in English or Norwegian. The church is open from mid-May to mid-September. On Saturdays, weddings may interrupt visits.

Next, walk to Heddal Bygdetun, the village’s open-air museum, just a few steps from the church. It has around 15 historic buildings dating from the Middle Ages to the 1930s. In Rambergstugo, a former home, the walls feature decorations painted in 1784 by Olav Hanssen. The site is unstaffed, so you can wander freely among the houses. To see the interiors, ask the museum about guided tours available by reservation.

days_plan.itin_title: Telemark in 4 Days: Rjukan, Heddal, and the Telemark Canal

visits.text: The E6 then E69 route crosses the Finnmark tundra—a treeless plateau where reindeer roam freely across the road. Plan to slow down: herds cross at all hours and they don't move aside quickly.
The North Cape Tunnel (Nordkapptunnelen) plunges 212m beneath the sea to reach the island of Magerøya—6.8km of undersea road tunnel. It's the gateway to Honningsvåg and North Cape.
Honningsvåg's colourful harbour, its roughly 2,800 inhabitants and its brightly coloured houses give a human scale to this far end of the continent.

The North Cape plateau stands 307 m above the Arctic Ocean: this is where the metal globe erected in 1978 rises, an iconic symbol of Europe's Far North. On a clear day, you look towards the North Pole with no intervening land except Svalbard, 2,100 km away. Allow for a return drive from Honningsvåg.

Nordkapphallen is largely carved into the rock: it houses a panoramic cinema showing the North Cape through the four seasons, an ecumenical chapel (Sankt Johanneskapell) and a permanent exhibition. Allow 1 hour to see everything - admission is charged. Also allow for a return drive from Honningsvåg.

Make the detour to Gjesvær to reach the cliffs of Gjesværstappan, one of Norway's largest seabird colonies - puffins, northern gannets and cormorants nest there in large numbers. From Honningsvåg, plan a return drive to Gjesvær, followed by a boat excursion to the cliffs. Boat excursions depart from the village.

activities.text: The road from Honningsvåg to North Cape crosses the island of Magerøya: a 34 km track winding among lakes, across tundra, and past sheep grazing freely along the roadside. In summer, not a tree blocks the horizon—the landscape is lunar and the sky immense.

From 13 May to 29 July, the sun does not set at the North Cape - it traces a complete circle around the horizon, bathing the cliff in permanent golden light. Stay until midnight to experience this spectacle from the cliff edge: few experiences compare. Allow for a return drive from Honningsvåg.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Norway Road Trip: Tromsø, Alta & North Cape
Northern Norway Road Trip: Tromsø, Alta & North Cape

visits.text: Hornøya is the easternmost point of mainland Norway, meaning Norway excluding the Svalbard archipelago. The island is even farther east than Istanbul. Vardø Lighthouse stands at its highest point, 65 m above the sea. Allow 15 minutes to walk there from the dock. From the top, the view extends over the Barents Sea and the bird colony. The neighboring island of Reinøya is closed to the public: just look at it from the path.

activities.text: Board a boat at Vardø’s harbor, behind the tourist office, for the 10-minute crossing to Hornøya, a seabird nature reserve. Atlantic puffins, black-legged kittiwakes, common murres, razorbills, and European shags nest on the cliff. You will also see thick-billed murres. A marked path passes very close to the nests: stay on it. Allow about 2 hours on the island.

days_plan.itin_title: Varanger in 4 Days: Kirkenes, Vardø, and Hamningberg

visits.text: The ferry crossing from Lysebotn to Forsand travels the entire length of Lysefjord from its inner end—you'll see the walls of Kjerag and Preikestolen as you look along the fjord. Allow about 1 hour 30 minutes for the crossing, depending on the schedule. Check departures in advance; they're limited.
Stroll through Forsand village at the foot of Lysefjord - a few colorful houses, a quiet harbor, and views of the fjord walls from the quay. A good break after the previous days' efforts.

activities.text: Flørli houses the world's longest wooden staircase: 4,444 steps climbing through an elevation difference of 740 m along the old hydroelectric pipeline built between 1917 and 1921. The hamlet has no road access—you must take the ferry. At the top, Lake Ternevatnet and a view looking down over Lysefjord; descend via the Rallarstien to complete the loop.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Norway Road Trip: Stavanger, Preikestolen, Lysefjord & the South Coast

visits.text: Rebuilt in 2013 after the 2011 fire, the Breheimsenteret echoes the shapes of crevasses, the cracks in a glacier, and seracs, the blocks of ice that stand where it fractures. It is a visitor center for Jostedalsbreen National Park, home to the largest glacier in mainland Europe. The exhibition shows how ice shaped the valleys. A film follows the glacier through the seasons. The restaurant overlooks Nigardsbreen. In 2026, the center was open daily from May 1 through September 30, with hours of 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. in peak summer; admission was 125 NOK.

Jostedal Church, with its long white wooden nave, dates from around 1660. It replaced earlier churches on the same site, including a stave church probably dating from the 13th century. It is still the valley’s parish church. No visiting hours are published: if the door is closed, limit your visit to the exterior, in the center of Jostedal village.

activities.text: Beneath your feet, the ice of Nigardsbreen is a deep blue: the excursion is called Kort Blåistur, “short blue ice walk.” This glacier is an arm of Jostedalsbreen, a tongue of ice descending toward the valley. Between 1700 and 1748, during very cold winters, it advanced about 4 km and crushed farms. Guides from Jostedalen Breførarlag lead the excursion: 4 hours 30 minutes, including 1 hour 30 minutes on the ice, for ages 12 and up, with the boat ride and equipment included. In 2026, it ran daily from May 15 through September 25.

days_plan.itin_title: Jostedalsbreen in 4 Days: Urnes, Fjærland, and Loen

visits.text: The temperature is around 0 °C inside Andersgrotta, the air-raid shelter dug beneath central Kirkenes in 1941. During World War II, the German army had a major base here: the town was bombed more than 300 times. The shelter could protect about 2,500 residents. The guided tour in English lasts 30 minutes, including a 10-minute film. It also takes in the statue of a Red Army soldier, erected in 1951 just above the shelter. Tours leave daily at 12:30 p.m. from the entrance, with prices starting at 350 NOK. The tour is not recommended for children under 12.

On October 25, 1944, when the Red Army liberated Kirkenes, only 13 houses were still standing. Grenselandmuseet, the borderland museum, tells the story of the war and life in the town before and after it. It also covers the Sydvaranger company’s iron mines and the culture of the Sámi, the Indigenous people of northern Scandinavia. A Soviet Ilyushin fighter plane is displayed in the war gallery. The museum is 1 km from the center. From June 20 to August 20, it is open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

activities.text: Norwegians sometimes call it “Stalin’s crab.” The red king crab, native to the Pacific, was released by the Soviet Union into the Murmansk fjord in the 1960s. It then spread west into Norway, where it was first spotted as early as 1977. Its leg span can reach 1.8 m. On a king crab safari from Kirkenes, a fast inflatable boat takes you out onto the fjord, followed by a crab meal, usually one crab for two people. Allow 3 hours and about 2,500 NOK per adult, with warm clothing provided.

If your flight leaves Kirkenes in the early afternoon, leave Vardø early: allow about 3 hours 30 minutes to drive to Kirkenes, retracing your route along the Varangerfjord. Kirkenes Høybuktmoen Airport is about 5 km from town. Allow extra time, as reindeer often cross the road. Return your rental car at the airport.

days_plan.itin_title: Varanger in 4 Days: Kirkenes, Vardø, and Hamningberg
Varanger in 4 Days: Kirkenes, Vardø, and Hamningberg

visits.text: Head straight to the Munch galleries at KODE, Bergen’s art museum. They are in the Rasmus Meyer building, beside the small lake in the city center. KODE describes its Edvard Munch collection as the third most important in the world. It includes Jealousy (1895) and Evening on Karl Johan Street (1892), named after Oslo’s main avenue. Save time for the Blumenthal Room, whose walls and ceiling were painted around 1760. Outside summer, the museum is closed on Mondays and Tuesdays; on weekends, it opens from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Bergen in 2 Days: Bryggen, Fløyen, Ulriken, and Grieg

visits.text: In 1947, six men crossed the Pacific on a raft made of balsa, a very lightweight wood. This raft, the Kon-Tiki, is on display at the Kon-Tiki Museum (Kon-Tiki Museet), near the Fram. Their leader, Norwegian Thor Heyerdahl, wanted to prove that peoples from South America could have reached Polynesia before Christopher Columbus arrived in the Americas. Setting off from Peru, they sailed for 101 days before striking a reef in the Tuamotu Islands in Polynesia. The museum also displays the Ra II, a reed boat that crossed the Atlantic in 1970. Allow 1 hour; admission is 180 NOK.

days_plan.itin_title: Oslo in 2 Days: MUNCH, Vigeland, the Opera House, and Bygdøy

visits.text: Posebyen, Kristiansand's historic quarter, survived the great fire of 1892 - the other neighborhoods burned, this one didn't. Founded in 1641 by King Christian IV, the city preserves its grid layout and single-story white wooden houses here. A peaceful atmosphere a stone's throw from the harbor.
Christiansholm fortress, completed in 1672 on an islet facing the harbor, was attacked only once, in 1807, by the British navy. Its walls are up to 5 m thick. Free entry, open April to October.
Fiskebrygga, Kristiansand's fish market, brings the waterfront to life with its boats and seafood stalls. A good vantage point for the harbor and the archipelago stretching out in front of the city.
Ravnedalen is a nature park right inside Kristiansand: ponds, waterfalls, and a small open-air stage amid the rocks. A quiet stroll 10 minutes' walk from the center, popular with locals.
Kristiansand Cathedral (Kristiansand domkirke), built in 1884 in neo-Gothic style, is Norway's third-largest church with 1,800 seats. You'll see its brick facade from the main square.

activities.text: Take a boat to explore Kristiansand's archipelago—small granite islands, colorful summer houses, and swimming in coves. In summer, regular services depart from the harbor for nearby islands.

The island of Bragdøya is accessible by boat from central Kristiansand in summer - coastal trails, rocky beaches and swimming in the calm waters of the archipelago. A perfect way to bring this road trip to a gentle close.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Norway Road Trip: Stavanger, Preikestolen, Lysefjord & the South Coast
Southern Norway Road Trip: Stavanger, Preikestolen, Lysefjord & the South Coast

visits.text: The village of Bud, at the entrance to the Atlantic Ocean Road, was the busiest trading center between Bergen and Trondheim in the 16th-17th centuries. Allow for a round trip during the day from Kristiansund. Today, a few dozen red wooden houses face the open ocean - the contrast with the raging Hustadvika is striking in stormy weather.

The Atlantic Ocean Road (Atlanterhavsveien) links small islands over 8.3 km with 8 bridges facing the Norwegian Sea - built between 1983 and 1989 after weathering 12 violent storms during construction. Allow for a round trip during the day from Kristiansund. It was voted Norway's “construction of the century” in 2005. In bad weather, waves literally wash over the bridges.

The Storseisundet Bridge, 260 meters long, is the most photographed bridge on the road. Allow for a round trip during the day from Kristiansund. Its cantilevered curve creates an optical illusion from certain angles: the road appears to plunge straight into the ocean. Stop at the viewing area for the photo - you cannot get it from the car.

activities.text: Drive the Atlantic Ocean Road as a round trip from Kristiansund. Plan frequent stops at the four designated viewpoints along the route.

days_plan.itin_title: Central Norway Road Trip: Ålesund, Geirangerfjord, Trollstigen & Trondheim

visits.text: The roar drowns out everything as soon as you open the car door: Låtefossen plunges right beside Rv13. It is a twin waterfall. Two torrents descend from Lake Lotevatnet and merge halfway down. The water then passes beneath an old stone bridge with six arches, after a total drop of 165 m. Visitors have been coming to see it since the 19th century: the first tourists arrived from Odda in horse-drawn carriages. The parking lot is free but small, and the bridge is narrow: in summer, arrive early to avoid traffic jams.

activities.text: You can see Låtefossen from above by taking the old stone-surfaced road that starts 50 to 60 m south of the bridge. It climbs the eastern slope to a viewpoint above the falls. The ruins of a former café with panoramic views remain at the top. Låtefossen is not the area’s only waterfall: the Odda valley is sometimes called “the valley of waterfalls.” Cross Rv13 carefully to reach the start of the trail, as the tourist office advises.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Hardanger in 3 Days: Trolltunga, Folgefonna, Rosendal

visits.text: The best starting point for understanding the Gudbrandsdal Valley is Maihaugen, Lillehammer’s large open-air museum. Dentist Anders Sandvig began collecting old houses from the valley in 1887. The museum opened at this site in 1904. Today, it has around 200 buildings. Among them, Garmo Church dates from the early 13th century. It is a stave church: its timber frame rests on large vertical posts. Allow 2 hours 30 minutes. In peak season, an adult ticket costs 235 NOK.

The Norwegian Olympic Museum (Norges olympiske museum) has been housed at Maihaugen since 2016. It tells the story of the Games from antiquity to the present through more than 7,000 objects. Two editions take center stage: the 1952 Oslo Winter Games and the 1994 Lillehammer Winter Games. The same ticket includes admission to Maihaugen and the Olympic Museum. Allow 1 hour for it at the end of your visit.

If you enjoy novels, visit Bjerkebæk, Sigrid Undset’s wooden home in Lillehammer. This Norwegian novelist received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1928. Her best-known work, Kristin Lavransdatter, is set in medieval Norway. She lived here from 1919. An opponent of the Nazis, she fled Norway during the German invasion in 1940 and returned in 1945. The house can only be visited on a guided tour, offered several times a day in summer: check the schedule before you go.

Wooden facades, bay windows, and gabled roofs: Storgata, Lillehammer’s main street, is lined with two-story wooden houses from the late 19th century. In 1827, the town was granted market town status, giving it the right to trade. Save this walk for the end of the day. Then head down toward Lake Mjøsa, Norway’s largest lake, with the town at its northern end.

activities.text: You can climb the 936 steps at the Lysgårdsbakken Olympic ski jumps or ride up on the chairlift. The opening and closing ceremonies of the 1994 Winter Games took place at the foot of these ski jumps. The large hill allows jumps of around 140 m. From the top, the views stretch across Lillehammer and Lake Mjøsa. The chairlift generally operates from May through September, and an adult ticket costs 80 NOK.

days_plan.itin_title: Norway’s Mountains in 5 Days: Lillehammer and Jotunheimen

visits.text: In 1905 and again in 1936, sections of Mount Ramnefjellet fell into Lake Lovatnet, which the road to Kjenndalsbreen follows. These rockfalls triggered giant waves, reaching up to 74 m in height in 1936. They leveled the hamlets of Bødal and Nesdal and killed 135 people in total. After a 17 km drive along the toll road from Loen, Kjenndalsbreen glacier is just a 15-minute walk from the parking lot. The road is closed in winter; the Kjenndalstova café opens from May through September.

activities.text: The fjord drops rapidly away beneath the Loen Skylift cabin: in about 5 minutes, it climbs 1,011 m, on a slope that reaches 60° in places. At the top, on Mount Hoven, the Skredfjellet trail (2 km one way, with 155 m of elevation gain) follows a gravel path suitable for all ages. In 2027, the cable car will run daily from May 1 through October 3, until 11 p.m. in July. Your ticket has no set return time: simply head back down before closing.

days_plan.itin_title: Jostedalsbreen in 4 Days: Urnes, Fjærland, and Loen

visits.text: Lom Stave Church has stood in the center of the village since the 12th century: the timber used for its frame was felled during the winter of 1157–1158. It was enlarged in 1634 and again in the 1660s, giving it its cross-shaped layout. The dragon heads on the roof are copies, and the originals are displayed near the parking lot. Excavations here in 1973 uncovered 2,245 coins, a record for a Norwegian church. Admission costs around 90 NOK, from June through September.

More than half of the archaeological objects found in ice worldwide come from the mountains around Lom. Norsk Fjellsenter, the Norwegian Mountain Center, displays around a hundred of them in its Frozen in Time exhibition. The cold preserved these objects for millennia, and melting ice is revealing them again. You will see a 6,000-year-old arrow and a Viking Age mitten. The center also welcomes visitors to Jotunheimen National Park: pick up maps and advice for Besseggen here.

Crystals, polished stones, and fossils fill the display cases at Fossheim Steinsenter, Lom’s stone center. Its collections bring together minerals from more than 700 Norwegian deposits. The center also displays a meteorite around 4.6 billion years old, which it presents as the oldest stone in the world. Outside the door, a pile of stones replenished daily awaits children, who can take some. Half an hour is enough.

For a break in Lom, nothing beats the banks of the Bøvra. In the village center, this river forms Prestfossen waterfall before joining the Otta River. On the banks of the same river, Bakeriet i Lom bakes its bread in two large wood-fired ovens. This bakery was founded by Morten Schakenda, a former fine-dining chef. Pick up a sandwich and settle in facing the water.

activities.text: Follow Bordvassvegen, an easy trail along an old irrigation canal above Lom. There is very little rain here: many parts of Lom and the neighboring municipality of Skjåk receive less than 300 mm a year. To grow crops, farmers dug canals to bring glacial meltwater to their fields. Lom has 68 canals and small dams, with canals totaling about 230 km in length. The trailhead sign is behind Norsk Fjellsenter, and the trail markings are red.

days_plan.itin_title: Norway’s Mountains in 5 Days: Lillehammer and Jotunheimen

visits.text: After the ferry crossing from Breivikeidet to Svensby, follow Route 91 along the Lyngenfjord: the Lyngen Alps rise above the fjord, with their rugged peaks and numerous glaciers. Stop at the viewpoints to enjoy the views of the mountains and their reflections in the fjord.

Lyngseidet is the main village on the Lyngen peninsula: a fjord on one side, glacier-carved rock faces on the other. This is where the ferry departs to cross the Lyngenfjord - allow approximately 40 minutes for the crossing.

activities.text: The hike to Blåisvatnet (Blue Lake) is the most popular in the Lyngen Alps: an 8 km round trip, 189 m of elevation gain, and relatively flat terrain apart from the final boulders before the lake. Its intense turquoise colour comes from meltwater from the Lenangsbreen glacier just above. Wear good footwear - the ground is stony throughout. From Lyngseidet, plan a return drive to the car park, followed by a hike to the lake.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Norway Road Trip: Tromsø, Alta & North Cape

visits.text: The road from Sirdal to Lysebotn crosses a mountain plateau where you might spot wild reindeer - keep your eyes on the roadside. The landscape changes dramatically as you descend toward the fjord.

Lysevegen: 27 dizzying switchbacks descend through an elevation difference of 640 m to reach the inner end of Lysefjord. Take your time on the bends—a few viewpoints let you grasp the scale of the descent.
Lysebotn has about ten permanent residents and serves as a base for BASE jumpers from around the world, drawn by Kjerag's walls. A place apart, at the end of the world, at the head of a fjord.

activities.text: Kjeragbolten is that 5 m³ boulder wedged between two cliffs 984 m above Lysefjord. The hike is 11 km round trip with 700 m elevation gain: metal chains on the steep sections help you climb, but the slabs can be slippery in wet weather. Allow 6 hours. Start early to avoid the queue at the boulder.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Norway Road Trip: Stavanger, Preikestolen, Lysefjord & the South Coast

visits.text: Flekkefjord and its Dutch quarter (Hollenderbyen) feature rows of white facades reminiscent of the North Sea's trading towns - this architecture reveals the old trading ties with the Netherlands. An easy stop along the way. From Mandal, allow approximately 66 km and 1 hour of driving.

Sjøsanden beach in Mandal, 800 m long, is regularly voted Norway's best beach. It stretches within the Furulunden nature park, a 10-minute walk from the center - fine sand, calm water, pine forest backdrop.
Mandal's old town spreads out west of the harbor, with its winding lanes and white wooden houses. The town is the birthplace of sculptor Gustav Vigeland, whose works adorn Oslo's large park.

activities.text: Lindesnes fyr is Norway's first lighthouse - the first lantern was lit here in 1656, and the current cast-iron tower dates from 1915. You are at the southernmost point of mainland Norway, 2 518 km from the North Cape. From Mandal, allow approximately 39 km and 40 minutes of driving to the parking lot. The coastal trail from the parking lot is a 3 km round trip with a few rocky sections.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Norway Road Trip: Stavanger, Preikestolen, Lysefjord & the South Coast

activities.text: Måtinden rises to just 408 m, but its summit drops sheer into the ocean. It is Andøya’s most visited mountain. The trail starts at a parking lot on the road between Stave and Bleik. It first crosses a peat bog, an area of spongy, waterlogged ground, before tackling its steepest, rockiest section. From the summit, the view takes in white beaches, the open sea, and Bleiksøya, the bird island. Allow 3 to 4 hours for the roughly 8 km round trip. At the top, stay well back from the cliff edge. Hike up in the evening to enjoy the midnight sun.

days_plan.itin_title: Vesterålen in 4 Days: Andenes Whales, Bleik, and Nyksund

visits.text: Modest, yet a survivor: the wooden church in Nesseby escaped the fires at the end of the war. As it retreated, the German army burned most buildings in Finnmark, and this church is one of the few older structures still standing. It was consecrated in 1858. Its prayer books are written in Northern Sámi. The church serves as a stopping point on the Varanger National Scenic Route, facing the fjord: a 30-minute break is enough.

11,000 years ago, the sea reached 70 m higher than it does today on the slope at Ceavccageađge, the Mortensnes cultural heritage site. Since the end of the Ice Age, the land, freed from the weight of the ice, has been slowly rising. This is why the oldest traces of settlement, dating back about 9,000 years, now lie 60 m above the water. The trails also lead to nearly 300 Sámi graves and a standing stone surrounded by 13 stone circles, an ancient offering site. Allow at least 1 hour for an easy walk.

days_plan.itin_title: Varanger in 4 Days: Kirkenes, Vardø, and Hamningberg

visits.text: If you are keen to see The Scream at MUNCH, the Edvard Munch museum, be aware that the version on display changes throughout the day. The museum owns eight versions: one painting, one drawing, and six lithographs (prints made from a drawing on stone). Light fades the colors and damages the paper, so none can remain on permanent display. They take turns on the 4th floor in the Edvard Munch Infinite exhibition. Then head up to the 13th and top floor for views over the city. Open until 9 p.m. Wednesday through Saturday; admission is 220 NOK.

days_plan.itin_title: Oslo in 2 Days: MUNCH, Vigeland, the Opera House, and Bygdøy

visits.text: The best starting point for a weekend in Oslo is the Nasjonalmuseet, the National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design. It opened in June 2022 behind the former West Station. Its Munch room brings together 18 major works by painter Edvard Munch, including the 1893 version of The Scream. On the top floor, the Lyshallen (“Light Hall”) has glass walls enclosing a thin layer of marble. In the evening, it glows like a lamp above the city. Closed on Mondays, the museum stays open until 8 p.m. on Tuesdays and Wednesdays.

days_plan.itin_title: Oslo in 2 Days: MUNCH, Vigeland, the Opera House, and Bygdøy

visits.text: Sea breezes, paths, and benches facing the fjord: Nordnesparken occupies the tip of the Nordnes peninsula, west of the city center. Look for the totem pole, a wooden pole carved in the style of the Indigenous peoples of North America’s Pacific Coast. Seattle, Bergen’s sister city, gave it in 1970 to mark the 900th anniversary of the city, traditionally said to have been founded in 1070. The more adventurous swim at Nordnes sjøbad, a heated seawater pool with a sauna, or directly in the sea.

days_plan.itin_title: Bergen in 2 Days: Bryggen, Fløyen, Ulriken, and Grieg

visits.text: Traditional music and warm flatbreads: from late June to mid-August, the Norsk Folkemuseum (Norwegian Museum of Cultural History) offers folk dancing every hour and lefse, a soft flatbread. This open-air museum has reassembled more than 150 buildings brought here from towns and rural areas. At its center stands Gol Stave Church, whose timber frame rests on large posts. Its tree rings, the rings a tree forms each year, date it to between 1157 and 1216. Admission is 200 NOK; from October to April, opening hours are 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Oslo in 2 Days: MUNCH, Vigeland, the Opera House, and Bygdøy

visits.text: The world’s first calcium nitrate factory began operating in Notodden in 1905, producing fertilizer for farmland. The World Heritage Center, housed in a former industrial hall at the Tinfos industrial site, tells the story of this invention. The Birkeland–Eyde process heated air to several thousand degrees using an electric arc, a kind of continuous lightning bolt. Nitrogen from the air was then turned into a fertilizer sold as Norgessalpeter. The same ticket includes admission to Telemark Kunstmuseum, the art museum that shares the hall. From June 22 to August 9, both are open daily from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Grønnbyen, literally “the green town,” is the workers’ housing district built by Hydro in the early 20th century. Its 25 duplex houses are divided vertically: each family had its own half, from the ground floor to the roof. Farther on, the Villamoen neighborhood has 17 villas built for engineers and managers in various styles, including Art Nouveau. At the far end stands Admini, the former home and office of Hydro founder Sam Eyde. It overlooks the factories and the lake. Hydro still uses it for meetings, so admire it from the street.

Despite its industrial roots, Notodden has become Norway’s blues town. Bok & Blueshuset, the “house of books and blues,” is its heart, housing a library, concert venues, and a tourist information office. The building rests on the concrete slab of Anlegg 5, a former industrial furnace hall. Founded in 1988, the Notodden Blues Festival attracts thousands of spectators each summer. The 2027 festival is scheduled for August 5 to 8: book your accommodations early if you plan to visit on those dates.

activities.text: Between large loading cranes and the waters of Lake Heddalsvatnet, Notodden’s industrial promenade follows the shoreline for 2 km. It begins near Hydroparken, Hydro’s former waterfront factories, where fertilizer production began. The path is flat and easy, suitable for all ages. Benches and lighting have been installed along the entire route, so the walk can also be taken in the evening after the museums close.

days_plan.itin_title: Telemark in 4 Days: Rjukan, Heddal, and the Telemark Canal

visits.text: Nusfjord is one of Norway's oldest fishing villages, with traces of human settlement dating back to 425 BC. In 1975, it was designated one of three UNESCO pilot projects in Norway for the preservation of traditional groups of wooden buildings. Today home to just 25 permanent residents, the village nonetheless welcomes 80,000 visitors per year. An entrance fee is charged in summer to contribute to site conservation.

Ramberg beach offers white sand with blue-green waters backed by mountains, the kind of panorama you'd expect more in the tropics. In July, you can swim here. Don't expect solitude: this is one of the most frequented beaches in the Lofoten in summer.

The Lofotr Viking Museum in Borg is approximately 37 km from Nusfjord, a 35-minute drive. It is built around the largest Viking longhouse ever discovered in Europe, unearthed in 1983 by a farmer ploughing his fields. The foundation measured 83 metres long and 9.5 metres wide, dated to around AD 500. The 1995 reconstruction lets you explore the interior, see replicas of Viking ships and watch craft demonstrations.

activities.text: The coastal trail from Nusfjord to Nesland runs past rocky coves and free-roaming sheep, with views over the fjord. Allow 2 hours 30 minutes for the 7 km round-trip, with no difficult elevation changes. The trail is poorly marked toward the end—download a GPS track before setting out.

days_plan.itin_title: Arctic Norway Road Trip: Tromsø, Senja & the Lofoten Islands

visits.text: Once a ghost village, now an artists’ haven: Nyksund has had two lives. Around 1900, it was Vesterålen’s second-largest fishing port, bustling with nearly 1,000 people during the fishing season. As boats grew larger, its narrow harbor could no longer accommodate them, and residents moved away. The last resident left the village in 1975. Nyksund occupies two islets, Ungsmaløy and Nyksundøy, connected by a causeway. Park in the parking lot at the entrance: the narrow, steep lanes are explored on foot.

activities.text: In 1985, young people from Berlin began bringing Nyksund back to life. Launched by German educator Karl Heinz Nickel, the project gave disadvantaged young people practical work: repainting, clearing debris, and repairing houses. For about ten years, hundreds of young Europeans took turns working here in summer. Today, artists and musicians live here. Stroll between the two art galleries and Delpen, a bookstore and café selling books from northern Norway and antiques.

visits.text: An industrial town at the foot of a glacier, Odda actually got its start in tourism: in the early 20th century, more than 80 cruise ships called here each season. Then electricity generated by the rushing streams attracted industry. From 1908 to the early 2000s, the Smelteverket plant (“the smelter”) produced carbide, a chemical substance partly processed into fertilizer. In 2009, Norway nominated this industrial heritage for UNESCO World Heritage status. The tourist office, at the bus station, is open weekdays from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.

In 1848, Lake Sandvinvatnet, south of Odda, partly inspired the setting of a famous Norwegian painting, “Bridal Procession on the Hardangerfjord.” It depicts a wedding procession crossing a fjord in rowboats. Adolph Tidemand painted the figures. Hans Gude painted the landscape, combining several places he had seen. Rv13 follows the lake’s eastern shore: pull into a turnout to look across at the valley rising toward Buarbreen Glacier.

visits.text: Five degrees year-round: that is the temperature awaiting you in Olavsgruva, Olav’s Mine, 13 km from Røros. The guided tour lasts about 1 hour and takes you through two mines. Excavation at Nyberget began in 1650, while Olavsgruva operated from 1936 to 1972. You descend 50 m underground and walk 500 m to Bergmannshallen, the “Miners’ Hall.” Bring a warm jacket and sturdy shoes, as the ground is slippery. Admission costs 220 kroner per adult.

The surface buildings at Olavsgruva also tell the mine’s story. The headframe, built over the shaft in 1936, also helped ventilate the mine. The café occupies a house from Bergmannsgata in Røros that was moved here in 1947. Pay particular attention to the 1946 ore ropeway: this aerial cable, about 1.3 km long, carried ore. Norway’s Directorate for Cultural Heritage describes it as the only intact example of its kind remaining in the country. Allow half an hour for the small exhibition on the region’s geology.

activities.text: If you have an extra hour, walk around the Storwartz mining field, the area of former mines surrounding Olav’s Mine. Nine mines were opened here, the first in 1645. In 1646, the king of Denmark–Norway granted the company all rights to minerals, forests, and rivers within a circle with a radius of about 45 km. This circle is called the Circumference. It gives its name to the UNESCO-listed site, “Røros Mining Town and the Circumference.” Its center is near here. Stay away from the old mine shafts.

visits.text: Completed in 1759, Old Olden Church (Gamle Olden kyrkje) has a Greek cross plan, with four equal arms. It is the only church with this layout in Nordfjord. It no longer serves as a parish church and operates as a small museum. It is only open to visitors in summer: check the posted hours before counting on a visit inside.

days_plan.itin_title: Jostedalsbreen in 4 Days: Urnes, Fjærland, and Loen

activities.text: You can walk on the roof of the Oslo Opera House (Operahuset): it slopes down to the level of the plaza, so you can walk up for views of the fjord. Inaugurated on April 12, 2008, the building was designed by Norwegian architecture firm Snøhetta. Its slopes are clad in white granite and white Italian marble. In the water, a glass and steel sculpture, She Lies, floats and moves with the tide and wind. Wear sneakers, as recommended by the Norwegian tourist board.

days_plan.itin_title: Oslo in 2 Days: MUNCH, Vigeland, the Opera House, and Bygdøy

visits.text: In 1794, boat skipper Elling Pedersen obtained permission to open a shop and an inn in Ørnes. Three buildings remain from this former trading post, Ørnes handelssted: the main house, the old bakery, and the forge. They have been protected since 1942. The site served as the village’s gathering place for many years. In 2026, it is open Monday through Saturday, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., from June 20 to August 8.

The most enjoyable way to spend time in Ørnes, the administrative center of Meløy municipality, is to stroll among the old harbor buildings. Several date from around 1800: houses, fishermen’s cabins, boathouses, barns, and a forge, some of which are protected. The island of Mesøya lies just west of the village. Hurtigruten calls here daily. Park near the dock and explore on foot in 30 minutes.

places.name: Oslo

visits.text: Follow the Akerselva from Grünerløkka to the waterfalls and old mills - 9.8 km of trail threading through Oslo's industrial history. In 1856, the river's 20 cascades powered around twenty textile factories and flour mills. Walk it north to south: the view of the Opera House and fjord comes at the end.

The waterfront at Aker Brygge and Tjuvholmen shows you two faces of Oslo along the Oslofjord: former shipyards converted into restaurants and galleries on one side, the contemporary jetty at Tjuvholmen on the other. Walk out to the end of the pier for views across the fjord islands.

Climb onto the marble roof of Oslo Opera House (Operahuset) - it's free, open all the time, and the view over the fjord is the best in the city. The building, designed by Snøhetta and opened in 2008, is clad in Carrara marble and white granite. It won the Mies van der Rohe Prize in 2009. Pack slip-resistant shoes in winter: the roof gets slippery.
Oslo's Botanical Garden (Botanisk hage), in Tøyen, has existed since 1814 and houses one of Europe's largest collections of Nordic plants. Admission to the outdoor garden is free.

The Barcode Project, in the Bjørvika district, lines up a series of towers with striped facades designed by different architecture firms between 2005 and 2016. View them from the waterfront promenade - the barcode effect reads more clearly from a distance.

Climb up to the Damstredet and Telthusbakken neighbourhood, a ten-minute walk from the centre: you'll find painted wooden houses from the 18th and 19th centuries that survived Oslo's successive rebuildings. A striking contrast with the glass towers down by the water.

Sagene, Oslo's former industrial heartland, is now one of the city's most sought-after neighbourhoods. The name comes from Old Norwegian 'sager', meaning sawmills - the first date back to the 16th century. Wander past red-brick facades and former warehouses now converted into workshops and cafés.

The Norsk Folkemuseum at Bygdøy gathers over 150 historic buildings relocated from across Norway - it's one of Europe's largest open-air museums. The centrepiece is the Gol Stave Church, built around 1200 in the Hallingdal valley. In 1880, the municipality of Gol wanted to demolish it to build a new one. The Society for the Preservation of Ancient Monuments bought it, and King Oscar II funded its transfer to Bygdøy in 1884. On one of the nave pillars, a runic inscription reads: “Kiss me, for I struggle.” Allow 2 hours to tour the whole museum.

The former Viking Ship Museum (Vikingskipshuset) is currently closed. It is due to reopen in November 2027 as the Museum of the Viking Age (Vikingtidsmuseet). The new museum will notably display the famous Oseberg, Gokstad and Tune Viking ships, along with sledges, textiles and objects discovered in Viking burials. The 9th-century Oseberg ship was discovered in 1904 in a burial mound near Tønsberg.

The Holmenkollen Ski Museum is the world's oldest ski museum - it opened in 1923 and traces 4,000 years of skiing history, from Stone Age rock carvings to the gear from Fridtjof Nansen and Roald Amundsen's polar expeditions. The facade was completely renovated by Snøhetta in 2023. The building is carved into the mountain, beneath the ski jump.

From the viewing platform atop Holmenkollbakken - a ski jump built in 1892 and rebuilt for the 1952 Oslo Olympics - you get the panoramic view of the city and Oslofjord that every guidebook describes. It deserves its reputation. Take the lift, then climb 114 steps to the top. Allow 30 to 40 minutes to explore the summit. Avoid competition days if you want the terrace to yourself.

On the RV7, the crossing of Hardangervidda gives you 67 km of lunar landscape - northern Europe's largest high-altitude plateau, at 1,100-1,200 metres. Lake after lake, open heath and infinite horizons. It's also one of the few places in Europe where wild reindeer migrate freely: several thousand animals cross the plateau with the seasons.
In Hol, stop to see Hol Gamle Kyrkje (Hol's old church). A brief stop of 15-20 minutes is enough to see the exterior and the historic cemetery.

activities.text: Photo walk through Sentrum: the colourful facades and heritage buildings of the historic centre are particularly photogenic late in the day when low-angle light cuts through the narrow streets. Head from City Hall towards Parliament for an hour of urban wandering.

Return ferry trip from Aker Brygge to Bygdøy - approximately 10 minutes across the Oslofjord. It is the most enjoyable way to reach the Bygdøy peninsula and its museums, with lovely views of the fjord's islands.

Holmenkollen hosts annual biathlon and ski jumping competitions at the national arena - dates vary according to the FIS and IBU calendars. When no competitions are taking place, the cross-country ski trails of Nordmarka start just behind the jump. Reach Holmenkollen by metro (line 1, Holmenkollen station, 25 minutes from the centre).

Return by car from Ulvik to Oslo via the RV7 and the E16: allow approximately 5 hours 5 minutes of driving, excluding breaks. Pass through Geilo to refuel if needed. Check conditions on vegvesen.no in autumn and spring: the RV7 can close during snowstorms on the plateau.

visits.text: Every hour from 7 a.m. to midnight, the 49 bells of Oslo City Hall (Oslo rådhus) play a tune above the harbor. The building was inaugurated in 1950 to mark the city’s 900th anniversary. Every December 10, it hosts the Nobel Peace Prize ceremony. In the main hall, murals by Henrik Sørensen and Alf Rolfsen depict the history and working lives of Norwegians. Entry is through a security check, Monday through Saturday from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. City Hall is closed on Sundays, so plan this first day for a Saturday.

visits.text: Reine is nestled between sharp peaks and the blue-green waters of the Reinefjorden—the most reproduced postcard image of the Lofoten. The light here is spectacular at any hour, but especially at dusk. Park at the harbor and explore the lanes around the rorbu on foot.

The Fredvang bridges span several small islands between Flakstad and Moskenesøy, with views down over the Selfjorden. Plan for the return drive from Reine. Stop by the roadside for a photo: the view of the arched bridges with the mountains behind them is one of the most photographed in the Lofoten Islands.

The hamlet of Hamnøy, 5 minutes from Reine, is home to the most photographed red rorbu in the Lofoten, facing the Reinefjorden and sheer rock walls. This is the most accessible sunset and midnight sun spot from Reine. Plan to be here early in the morning or late in the evening to avoid groups of photographers.

Å i Lofoten is the last village at the end of the E10 road. Its name is a single letter meaning “river” in Old Norse. This was the end of the road at the edge of the world before modern tunnels. The Fishing Village Museum (Norsk Fiskeværsmuseum), founded in 1988, brings together several period buildings including a cod liver oil factory still in working order and an 1878 bakery. In summer, cinnamon rolls fresh from the stone oven await you here.

The Stockfish Museum (Lofoten Tørrfiskmuseum), set in a former fish landing hall, explains the entire cod-drying process—from fishing in January to export to Italy. Lofoten stockfish is now a protected designation at the European level, just like Roquefort. If you've seen cod-drying racks all along the route, this is where you'll understand why.

Reine is often described as Norway's most beautiful village—hard to dispute when you arrive by road and the red cabins on stilts suddenly appear facing the peaks plunging into Reinefjord. Reine's rorbuer, painted red, were once the lodgings of fishermen who came from the mainland to fish for cod from January to April. Many have been converted into accommodations—book well in advance.

A few kilometres away, the village of Å (pronounced “Ô”) marks the end of the road. This remote spot can be explored like an open-air museum: a boathouse, a cod-liver oil factory, a forge, a former post office and rorbuer. The Norwegian Fishing Village Museum traces the history of cod fishing in 7 buildings. Do not miss Hamnøy: the red cabins seen from the bridge may be the best-known photograph of the Lofoten Islands.

Kvalvika beach is one of the most beautiful in the Lofoten Islands: a white-sand cove ringed by 400-metre peaks that plunge into the Arctic. From Reine, plan a day trip by car to the Fredvang parking area and back. You then reach the beach on foot, with a 1-hour walk to the beach along a marked trail. Bring waterproof footwear. Along the way, the Fredvang bridges - two suspension bridges over a strait between three islands - are among the most popular photo spots in the Lofoten Islands.

In the late afternoon, take the detour to Nusfjord, approximately 41 km from Reine, a 40-minute drive. It is one of the best-preserved fishing villages in the Lofoten Islands, tucked away at the head of a fjord. There is an admission fee, but it gives you access to a village that seems straight out of the 1900s. Take the path that climbs at the entrance for a panoramic view before heading down to stroll along the pier.

activities.text: Reinebringen is the most famous hike in the Lofoten, with 1,978 stone steps built by Nepalese Sherpas between 2016 and 2021 to stabilize the trail. The summit reaches 448 meters, with a view down over Reine, Hamnøy, and the Reinefjorden. Allow 2 hours 30 minutes to 3 hours round-trip. Avoid it in wet weather—the steps become slippery and the view disappears. In July, start before 8 a.m. to avoid lines on the trail.

The hike to the hidden beach of Kvalvika from Fredvang crosses moorland and low ridges with views of the Selfjord. From Reine, plan a return drive to the trailhead near Fredvang, then continue on foot. The beach, accessible only on foot, remains wild and little visited outside July. Allow 3 hours for the 6 km round trip.

Sea kayaking between the small islands of the Reinefjorden is an ideal evening activity - from late May to mid-July, you paddle under the midnight sun between rock faces plunging straight into the water. Operators offer rentals and guided trips departing from Reine.

The Reinebringen hike (448 m) is the most famous in the Lofoten. The ascent is on a staircase of 1,600 stone steps laid in 2019 by Nepalese workers accustomed to Himalayan trails. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours for the ascent. At the summit, the view down over the Reinefjord, Kjerkfjord and Vorfjord with the red cabins below is the most photographed panorama in the Lofoten. Leave early—the parking lot fills up quickly in season.

Spend the morning on Rambergstranda or Skagsanden beach, two white-sand beaches easily accessible from the road. From Reine, plan a day trip by car to these beaches and back. In fine weather, the reflection of the mountains in the water is striking. The water is cold, but some people swim here in summer.
