visits.text: A medieval timber frame and a 17th-century bell tower: Ringebu Stave Church brings together two eras. It dates from around 1220. Around 1630, carpenter Werner Olsen enlarged it into a cross-shaped church, then added the red bell tower in 1631. Inside, a statue of Saint Lawrence dates from the 13th century. The church is open to visitors from June through August for a small admission fee, and its grounds remain freely accessible year-round.

days_plan.itin_title: Norway’s Mountains in 5 Days: Lillehammer and Jotunheimen

visits.text: If you arrive via Andøybrua, the 750 m bridge leading to the village of Risøyhamn, look down at the strait below. According to local tradition, it was once so shallow that people crossed it on horseback at low tide. To let ships through, a channel nearly 5 km long, the Risøyrenna, was dredged and opened in 1922. Richard With, founder of Hurtigruten, the Norwegian coastal shipping line, had long called for this channel. A 15-minute stop in the village is enough.

activities.text: Take your time driving the Andøya National Scenic Route (Nasjonal turistveg Andøya), which begins in Bjørnskinn, very close to the bridge. For 58 km to Andenes, it follows the west coast between the mountains and the ocean. Seals, whales, and white-tailed eagles, large sea eagles, can sometimes be seen from the car. Stop at designated rest areas such as Kleivodden, from which you can see Bleik and the island of Bleiksøya. Near Børvågen, operations at the Andøya Spaceport satellite launch facility can close the road for up to 8 hours.

days_plan.itin_title: Vesterålen in 4 Days: Andenes Whales, Bleik, and Nyksund

visits.text: Vemork was the world’s largest power station when it opened in 1911. It houses Norsk Industriarbeidermuseum, the Norwegian Industrial Workers Museum. Its World Heritage Center explains the 2015 UNESCO designation. In Rjukan and Notodden, Norsk Hydro harnessed the power of waterfalls to make fertilizer from nitrogen in the air. The power stations, factories, railways, and workers’ housing districts are listed together. From late June to mid-September, the museum is open daily from noon to 6 p.m. Park at Vemork Bridge, then allow 20 minutes for the steep walk.

On the night of February 27–28, 1943, Norwegian commandos blew up Vemork’s heavy water cellar, in the basement of the hydrogen plant. Heavy water looks like ordinary water, but its hydrogen atoms are heavier. In a nuclear reactor, it slows the particles that sustain the chain reaction. Nazi Germany needed it for atomic research. The sabotage destroyed more than 500 kg of heavy water and halted production for several months. Rediscovered intact by archaeologists, the cellar has been open to visitors since 2022. Admission is included in the Vemork ticket.

Rjukan takes its name from a waterfall you will probably see almost dry: Rjukanfossen. Its largest drop measures 104 m. However, Norsk Hydro diverted its water to supply its power stations. The waterfall therefore only flows fully when the upstream Møsvatn reservoir has excess water. Water is also released for the Marispelet performance, held over four days in July. Park in the parking areas east of the Maristi Tunnel, upstream from Vemork. The trail around the mountainside opens up views of the gorge after about 250 m.

activities.text: Nothing tells Hydro’s story better than a walk through central Rjukan. The town was built almost from scratch in the 1910s and 1920s. Start at Torget, the market square. From September to March, the sun stays too low to rise above the surrounding mountains, including Gaustatoppen, leaving the town without any direct sunlight. Stop by Rjukan Church, consecrated in 1915. In 1965, a fire destroyed its interior during the filming of The Heroes of Telemark. It was consecrated again in 1968.

Climb up to Solspeilet, Rjukan’s sun mirrors, installed in 2013 on the slope north of town, about 450 m above it. These three computer-controlled mirrors rotate to follow the sun. In winter, they reflect its light onto Torget, creating a patch of sunlight in the square. Hydro founder Sam Eyde proposed the idea back in 1913 but never brought it to life. The trail starts on the west side of town and runs about 1.7 km to the mirrors. It is steep, so bring sturdy shoes and water.

visits.text: The best starting point for understanding Røros is Smelthytta, the former copper smelter turned museum. From 1644 to 1977, the town depended on copper extracted from nearby mines. The ore, rock containing a small amount of metal, was first heated to drive off sulfur, then smelted here. These two stages consumed enormous quantities of wood. The current building, rebuilt in 1988, recreates the appearance of the 1888 smelter, which was destroyed by fire in 1953. The museum opens daily. Pick up the French audio guide, which is included in the ticket.

These dark hills on the edge of town are entirely human-made. Slegghaugan consists of slag heaps: the waste rock left after copper was smelted. Three centuries of smelting piled them up just steps from Smelthytta. They are now protected under Norway’s Cultural Heritage Act. Climb to the top for views across the town’s wooden rooftops and its whitewashed church.

Farmyards hide behind the wooden facades along Bergmannsgata, “Miners’ Street.” The street’s layout dates to the 17th century, shortly after the town was founded. A typical house also sheltered four to six cows: miners’ families partly supported themselves by raising livestock. UNESCO specifically recognizes this adaptation to a harsh, isolated life. Walk the street from end to end, then head to Kjerkgata, Røros’s other main street.

If you are wondering why Røros has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1980, Kjerkgata, “Church Street,” provides the answer. Swedish troops burned the town in 1678 and 1679. It was then rebuilt in wood. After the mining company went bankrupt in 1977, almost nothing was altered. Along this commercial street, each property combined a farm, a trading house, and living quarters. Follow it uphill toward the church that gave it its name.

It is nicknamed Bergstadens Ziir, “the ornament of the mining town.” Completed in 1784, Røros Church seats about 1,600 people, making it one of Norway’s largest churches. The mining company paid 23,000 riksdaler, the currency of the time, for it—equivalent to about 450 years of a miner’s wages. Inside, the altar is at the bottom, the pulpit above it, and the organ at the very top. The king had his own box above the entrance, while the poorest people sat in the galleries. In summer, the church opens Tuesday through Saturday, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Small, poor, yet famous: Sleggveien is one of Røros’s most modest streets. Its houses, built around 1840–1850 partly from salvaged materials, had neither barns nor cowsheds. Day laborers, poor widows, and single mothers lived here. It is also called “Pippi’s Street,” because an episode of Pippi Longstocking was filmed here. The street ends at the foot of Slegghaugan: climb the slag heaps to see it from above.

Day and night, the Røros smelter never stopped. Hytteklokka, the smelter bell, set the rhythm of this work: it rang at the end of each shift, when one crew of workers gave way to the next. Its current bell tower dates to the 1890s. The Hyttelva River, right beside it, explains the smelter’s location: the first one was built in 1646 near its waterfall. Look for the bell tower as you walk along the river near Smelthytta.

activities.text: You will gain a better understanding of Røros on the guided town tour organized by Rørosmuseet. It starts at Smelthytta, on Malmplassen square, and ends inside the church. Allow about 1 hour 20 minutes. From late June to mid-August, a Norwegian-language tour departs daily at 11 a.m., and an English-language tour at 1 p.m. Tickets cost 160 kroner per adult, and accompanied children under 16 enter free.

visits.text: The Barony of Rosendal (Baroniet Rosendal) alone makes this stop worthwhile. It is the only barony Norway has ever had. Ludvig Rosenkrantz built this manor house between 1661 and 1665. In 1678, King Christian V, who ruled Denmark and Norway, attached a baronial title to the estate. In 1927, the last owner donated it to the University of Oslo. Guided tours of the manor house: from June 22 to August 9, 2026, tours depart daily from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., with less frequent departures in May, June, and late August. Garden and manor house ticket: 210 NOK.

The scent of roses lingers into fall: in Rosendal Have, the Barony’s garden, around 2,000 rosebushes bloom from June to November. The Renaissance garden and its rose beds are about 300 years old. Around them, a Romantic landscape park was laid out around 1850, with a stone tower beside a pond. The garden remains open year-round, with garden-only admission costing 150 NOK. Take a break in the old kitchen (Gamlakjøkenet), which serves lappar, small Norwegian pancakes, with coffee.

Kvinnherad Church (Kvinnherad kyrkje) is a white stone church built in the mid-13th century in the heart of Rosendal. In 1678, it became part of the new barony’s estate. Many members of the Rosenkrantz family, the lords of the manor, are buried here. In season, guided tours of the church are available: ask at the Barony’s reception desk for times.

An outdoor geology museum or a playground? Rosendal’s Steinparken, the “stone park,” is a bit of both. Sculptor Bård Breivik and stonemason Rolf Karlsen shaped large blocks here amid a collection of rocks from the region. Waterwheels and pools where children can sail small boats keep them entertained. The park also tells the story of life on Earth and fossils. Admission is free year-round; the Dinosaur House (Dinosaurhuset) has its own opening hours.

If it rains in Rosendal, head to the Folgefonnsenteret on the dock: this exhibition center is devoted to Folgefonna National Park. Its galleries follow the journey of water from the glacier to the fjord. They also show how a warming climate is changing these landscapes. Four nature films round out the visit, including one about life beneath the surface of the fjord. Admission is 125 NOK. The tourist office, in the same building, is open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. through August 31.

visits.text: Step through the doorway of a 65 m longhouse at Høvdingsetet på Sandnes, a reconstructed Viking chieftain's estate less than a kilometer from downtown Sandnessjøen. A longhouse is the large wooden house typical of the Viking Age. This one was rebuilt on the site of the Viking Age building. The Sandnes estate appears in Egil's Saga, an Icelandic narrative. The site opens at set times in summer and by appointment for groups during the rest of the year.

Large murals decorate downtown Sandnessjøen, including Future Eyes, created in 2016 by Jort Agoch and Leticia Cascone Ruiz. Along the way, you will pass statues of Petter Dass and the Seven Sisters. Kulturbadet, which opened that same year, houses a swimming pool, movie theater, and library. One street is named after Torolv Kveldulvsson, a Viking chieftain who exported stockfish, or air-dried fish. Park near the harbor and explore downtown on foot.

At 1,065 m long, Helgelandsbrua, the Helgeland Bridge, has connected the island of Alsta, where Sandnessjøen is located, to the mainland since July 1991. It is a cable-stayed bridge: cables stretched from tall pylons support the roadway. Its longest span measures 425 m. Boats have up to 45 m of clearance beneath the roadway. You will cross it as you leave Sandnessjøen for the Levang ferry, and the crossing has been toll-free since 2005.

visits.text: Open flames were forbidden in Bryggen’s wooden houses for fear of fire. The merchants of the Hanseatic League therefore cooked and ate together at Schøtstuene, their assembly halls. Justice was also administered here. Bergen’s tourist office describes them as the last halls of their kind in the world. Beneath a glass floor, you can see the remains of a building dating from around 1280. Admission: 160 kroner. The neighboring St. Mary’s Church (Mariakirken), the city’s oldest building, generally opens only on certain weekdays, around noon.

days_plan.itin_title: Bergen in 2 Days: Bryggen, Fløyen, Ulriken, and Grieg

visits.text: The Senja National Scenic Route (Nasjonal turistveg Senja) connects Gryllefjord in the west to Botnhamn in the north. This is the route Norwegians themselves call the most beautiful in the national network. Take your time: every bend reveals cliffs 700 to 800 meters tall plunging straight into the Atlantic, hidden coves, and isolated villages.

Husøy is an active fishing village perched on its own islet in the Øyfjorden, connected to Senja by a 300-meter causeway. The colorful houses are anchored with cables to the ground to withstand storms. Local legend has it that the custom of the midday siesta, still practiced here, was introduced by Spanish Armada sailors shipwrecked on these shores in 1588.

The Bergsbotn viewing platform is cantilevered over the Bergsfjorden and is easily reached from the road. It frames the fjord and ridges like a painting. Be wary of the road leading up to it—it's very narrow, with motorhomes coming the other way.

From Tungeneset beach, a Siberian larch boardwalk crosses the rocks toward a promontory facing the Okshornan—the Devil's Teeth, three granite peaks rising from the ocean. Pools on the rocks reflect the summits in calm weather: bring a tripod for your photos. It's also one of the island's best spots for northern lights at night.

Ersfjordstranda beach is a strip of white sand framed by steep mountains—the kind of landscape you don't expect at this latitude. Don't miss the famous golden cabin: the gold-colored stainless steel public toilet, which has become an attraction in its own right on the island.

activities.text: Ferry crossing from Tromsø to Senja via the Brensholmen–Botnhamn route—about a 45-minute link that drops you directly at the start of the scenic route. The drive from Tromsø to Brensholmen takes about 1 hour. Arrive early at Botnhamn to start the scenic route in morning light.

activities.text: Head to Skien, a 30-minute drive from Ulefoss, for your fourth night. This is where the Telemark Canal begins: Skien Lock, the first of eight lock stations, raises boats just 5 m. Canal boats depart from the Hjellebrygga quay. The playwright Henrik Ibsen was born in this city. The next day, depart from Skien station, about 1 km from the center.

places.name: Skjaerhalden

visits.text: The Ytre Hvaler National Park visitor center occupies the Kornmagasinet, the former grain storehouse in Skjærhalden’s harbor. Established in 2009, this was Norway’s first marine national park. Of its 354 km², only 14 are land: all the rest lies beneath the sea. Among its protected features is the 1,200 m-long Tisler coral reef. The center’s exhibition explains this underwater world. From early June to mid-August, the center is open daily from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

With its rectangular stone nave and narrow chancel ending in a rounded apse, Hvaler kirke, or Hvaler Church, has the simple appearance of a medieval church. Construction probably began between the years 1000 and 1100. The church gave the island of Kirkøy its name, meaning “Church Island.” Inside, the pulpit dates from the 1600s and the altarpiece from 1759. Save your visit for late in the day, after the coastal trail.

activities.text: Set aside the afternoon for the Kyststien, Kirkøy’s coastal trail: an 11.4 km loop starting at the national park visitor center in Skjærhalden. Blue trail markers lead to Homlungen Lighthouse, a protected monument, then to Storesand Beach and its summer snack bar. The trail then crosses the old pine forest of Prestegårdsskogen, a nature reserve. At Rødshue, a former quarry displays works by five international sculptors. Allow about 3 hours of walking on sand, smooth rocks, and forest paths.

activities.text: You’ll land at Sogndal Airport (Haukåsen), served by Widerøe flights from Oslo and Bergen. Express boats also travel from Bergen up the Sognefjord to Sogndal. Continue the itinerary by car: follow road Fv55 for 17 km to Solvorn, on the Lustrafjord, the innermost arm of the Sognefjord. From there, a small ferry crosses to Ornes, the landing for Urnes Church. It holds only about ten cars, so cross on foot, as the church is just a short walk uphill from the landing.

visits.text: At 1,434 m, Fantesteinen marks the highest point on the Sognefjellet road. The official Norwegian Scenic Routes website describes it as the highest road pass in Northern Europe. The modern road opened in 1938. In the mid-1930s, young unemployed workers had dug part of it using shovels, pickaxes, and wheelbarrows. In spring, walls of snow nearly 10 m high still line the road. In July, afternoon temperatures average barely 11 °C: bring a jacket.

A sculpted block of stone stands out against the bare plateau: it is a work by artist Knut Wold at the Mefjellet rest area. This stop on the Sognefjellet road lies in the middle of the plateau. On a clear day, you can see the Fannaråken glacier and nearby peaks. Stop for 15 minutes: the rest area is wheelchair accessible.

In our opinion, Oscarshaug offers the finest view along the Sognefjellet road. The site is named after King Oscar II, who crossed the mountain in 1860. A cairn, a pile of stones used as a landmark, was erected to commemorate his passage. A path with a steel handrail leads there from the parking lot. Across from you, you will see the Hurrungane massif and the peak of Store Skagastølstind. Turn around here or at Turtagrø, 66 km from Lom, for the return trip.

activities.text: If the sky is clear, start with Galdhøpiggvegen, the toll road that climbs from Galdesand, at 550 m, to Juvasshytta, at the end of the road at 1,841 m. It gains about 1,300 m over 15 km. It is the highest paved road in Northern Europe: it climbs higher than Sognefjellet, but ends in a dead end without crossing a pass. Juvasshytta is a starting point for Galdhøpiggen, Northern Europe’s highest peak at 2,469 m.

visits.text: Two figures among the Begby carvings have names: Begbymannen, “the Begby Man,” and Danseren, “the Dancer.” These rock carvings, images cut into the rock, date from the early Bronze Age. You will also see an animal-shaped boat, carts, and suns. Begby is part of the Oldtidsruta, a series of signposted prehistoric sites along Route 110.

In the shade of the forest, a narrow trail leads to the Hornnes rock carvings. They depict 22 “solar boats,” carved in the early Bronze Age. At that time, the boat was the most important symbol. Wear closed-toe shoes: the trail can be wet.

The Solberg site is the easiest to view: it sits beside Route 110, with parking and interpretive signs. Its rock carvings depict four-wheeled carts, a large tree and a small one, and images of the sun. Some of the lines have been painted to make them easier to see. Avoid November through March: during the freezing season, most of the rock carvings along the Oldtidsruta are covered.

visits.text: A small village today, Solvorn was once the market town for everyone living along the shores of Lake Hafslovatnet. The town also housed a courthouse. Its heyday came when the fjord served as the main highway. When road Fv55 was built higher up toward Hafslo, traffic bypassed Solvorn. Stroll from the landing, where a ferry has departed for Ornes since 1859, to the church built in 1883, just above the houses.

activities.text: You can rent a kayak in Solvorn and paddle on the Lustrafjord, across from Urnes Church. A guesthouse in the village rents single and double kayaks, with paddles and life jackets, for 500 NOK for 4 hours. It also rents bicycles for 400 NOK per day. On the water, keep your life jacket on, stay close to shore, and head back if the wind picks up.

visits.text: From pale blue to deep blue, Sortland’s facades display every shade of a single color. This art project is called Blåbyen, “the blue town.” The idea came from a local artist, Bjørn Elvenes. The mayor presented it in 1998, and the municipality then adopted it as its project for the year 2000, despite residents’ initially mixed reactions. On some walls, look for short poems written by children and Lars Saabye Christensen, one of Norway’s best-known writers. An hour on foot is enough to explore the town center.

Look for the white bell tower rising south of the quay: it belongs to Sortland Church (Sortland kirke). A succession of places of worship has stood on this site since the 14th century. The current building dates from 1901. Its white exterior contrasts with the blue facades of the town center, making it a useful landmark for finding your way around. Allow about twenty minutes, before or after the walk toward the bridge.

activities.text: The opening of the Sortland Bridge (Sortlandsbrua) in 1975 greatly improved access to the entire region. It connects Langøya, the island where the town stands, to Hinnøya, the largest island in the archipelago. Walk along the waterfront to see both the bridge and the blue facades, which are visible from far out in the strait. Every day, the Hurtigruten coastal ship, which serves ports along the Norwegian coast, calls at Sortland: 15 minutes northbound and 30 minutes southbound.

visits.text: Step into Gamle Stavanger, Norway's best-preserved old quarter: 173 white wooden houses from the 18th and 19th centuries, flower-filled facades, and cobbled lanes. Allow a good hour to explore - this is a living residential neighborhood, not a frozen museum piece.

Stavanger Cathedral (Stavanger domkirke), founded around 1125, is Norway's oldest cathedral still in active use. The original Romanesque nave contrasts with the Gothic choir rebuilt after the 1272 fire—a fine example of architecture from two periods.

Øvre Holmegate, nicknamed the "street of colors" (Fargegaten), brings together brightly painted facades and a handful of trendy cafes. A striking contrast to the white houses of Gamle Stavanger, just a stone's throw away.

The Norwegian Petroleum Museum traces the oil saga from the discovery of the first North Sea fields in the 1960s. The building itself, opened in 1999, resembles an oil platform set in the harbor—you can't miss it.
The Norwegian Canning Museum occupies a converted sardine factory: you'll see cans being smoked on-site and understand how this industry built the city before oil took over. A packed half-hour.
The Stavanger Museum houses collections of natural history and regional archaeology, including Viking Age artifacts. Handy for preparing for tomorrow's hike with some regional context.

From the boat, you'll see Preikestolen from a completely different angle - the platform looks tiny against the 600 m of sheer wall. Many say it's even more impressive seen from below than from the summit.
Hengjanefossen waterfall plunges directly into the fjord from the cliffs: visible from the boat deck, it alone illustrates the immensity of Lysefjord.
Fantahålå cave (Vagabond's Cave) extends into the cliffs halfway up—the cruise guide will tell you when to look for it from the deck.

activities.text: Stroll from Vågen harbor to the fish market (Fisketorget): fresh shrimp, smoked salmon, and the maritime atmosphere of Stavanger's waterfront. The trick here is to arrive early for the best shrimp.

The Preikestolen hike is one of Norway's most famous: an 8 km round trip with 500 m of elevation gain, reaching a 25x25 m platform suspended 604 m above the Lysefjord. Set off before 7 a.m. - more than 300 000 hikers visit each year, and the daytime crowds can be overwhelming. From Stavanger, drive to the parking lot at Preikestolen fjellstue, where the hike starts.

The Lysefjord cruise from Stavanger travels the 42 km length of the fjord between cliffs that plunge from heights of up to 1,000 m. Allow 3 hours round trip. Book ahead in high season—boats depart in the morning from Stavanger harbor.

visits.text: Stø is a fishing village at the northernmost tip of Langøya, where the road ends facing the open sea. A radar station is visible on the nearby mountain. Offshore lies the Stø and Nyksund Nature Reserve, an important nesting site for seabirds. Walk around the harbor before setting off on your hike. If you prefer the sea to hiking, Arctic Whale Tours offers a 6 to 8 hour whale-watching day trip from June through August, departing at 10 a.m.

activities.text: Norwegians call it Dronningruta, “the Queen’s Route,” because Queen Sonja first hiked it in 1994. From Stø, this 12.3 km loop initially follows the coast, passing white-sand beaches and Skipssanden Beach. It then climbs onto a ridge to Finngamheia, its highest point, before descending back to the village. Allow about 5 hours of hiking, with 665 m of elevation gain. There are no springs along the route: bring enough water.

visits.text: Svolvær harbor is packed with rorbu—the iconic red wooden fishermen's cabins on stilts of the Lofoten. Walk out onto the Svinøya quay to see the cod-drying racks lined up on the rocks and the statue of the Fisherman's Wife (Fiskerkona). This is the natural crossroads of the archipelago before plunging south.

The Gunnar Berg Gallery at Svinøya displays the work of the painter born in Svolvær in 1863. His most famous painting depicts the Battle of Trollfjord in 1890—a revolt by small-scale fishermen in rowboats against industrial steamships blocking the entrance to the fjord with their nets. This painting became a national political symbol and contributed to the passage of the Lofoten fishing law.

Henningsvær is a fishing village of 510 inhabitants spread across several small islands linked by bridges, approximately 24 km from Svolvær, a 25-minute drive. Its football pitch is more famous than the village itself: carved into the rock since 1927, surrounded by sea on all sides and sheer peaks, it is the most photographed amateur stadium in the world. Climb the rock south of the pitch for the best view.

The KaviarFactory in Henningsvær is a former cod roe factory converted into an international contemporary art gallery. Allow approximately 24 km from Svolvær, a 25-minute drive. It has become one of Norway's most unexpected art venues. Go inside even if contemporary art is not your priority: the industrial building on the waterfront is worth a look.
The white-sand beach of Rørvikstranda has clear waters. You can swim there in July - the water reaches 15 to 17°C.

Kabelvåg Church (Vågan kirke), built in 1898, is nicknamed the Lofoten Cathedral—with 1,200 seats, it's the largest wooden church in northern Norway. It was built to accommodate the thousands of seasonal fishermen who converged on Kabelvåg in winter. Visit in the early morning: it's often open and not crowded.

The Lofoten Aquarium (Lofotakvariet) in Kabelvåg presents local marine wildlife in outdoor and indoor tanks: otters, seals and fish from Arctic fjords. It is a good option for families or when the weather rules out hiking.

Kabelvåg is historically the first commercial center of the Lofoten, founded in the 12th century by King Øystein Magnusson who built a shelter for fishermen there—making it one of the first towns in northern Norway. Stroll through the old center around the harbor: the 19th-century wooden houses are well preserved.

Welcome to the Lofoten. The Narvik–Svolvær route via the E10 (3–4 hours) is an experience in itself: it runs along fjords, passes through tunnels carved into rock and crosses suspension bridges between islands. Svolvær, the de facto capital of the Lofoten with 5,000 inhabitants, lives to the rhythm of its harbor. Head down to the quays: fishing boats, cod drying racks, rorbuer on stilts reflecting in the water. Skrei fishing (Arctic cod) remains the archipelago's engine—between January and April, Svolvær sees the world's largest cod catches.

Look up from the harbor: the Svolværgeita dominates the city from the flank of Mount Fløyfjellet. These two 150-meter rock pinnacles, nicknamed “the Svolvær Goat,” are the city's emblem. Climbers from around the world come to scale them. For the view without ropes, climb to Fløya (590 m, 2 hours from the center)—a guaranteed 360° panorama over the archipelago.

Step inside the Gunnar Berg Gallery, dedicated to the painter born here in 1863. His canvases capture the light of the Lofoten in the 19th century—stormy skies, reflections on water, fishermen's silhouettes. A way to understand these landscapes beyond photographs.

activities.text: The mini-cruise into Trollfjorden is the must-do excursion from Svolvær. This arm of the sea measures only 2.5 km long by 100 meters wide at the entrance, framed by walls exceeding 1,000 meters—Trolltindan peaks at 1,084 m. Operators offer daily departures in silent electric boats or fast RIBs. Book an early-morning departure for the best light on the cliffs.

The Festvågtind hike above Henningsvær offers a bird's-eye view of the village's small islands and their bridges. From Svolvær, plan a return drive to the trailhead near Henningsvær, then continue on foot. The uphill trail is approximately 5 km round trip with 490 metres of elevation gain. Allow 3 hours for an average walker. The route to the summit is not marked throughout - hiking boots are essential; avoid it in wet weather.

The Fløya hike above Svolvær is an accessible alternative to climbing Svolværgeita (the two iconic rock horns reserved for experienced climbers). The round-trip hike to Fløya takes 2 hours over 4 km and offers a view over the harbor, islets, and surrounding mountains. Start early in the morning to enjoy the panorama before the afternoon clouds.

Take a speedboat excursion to Trollfjord, a 2 km fjord arm squeezed between vertical granite walls - so narrow that large boats can barely maneuver there. This is also where white-tailed eagles, with their wingspan of over 2 meters, dive to catch fish. Operators offer this outing departing from the harbor.

activities.text: Few mountains can be walked through: Torghatten is one of them. This 258 m peak is pierced by a natural tunnel 160 m long and 35 m high. During the ice ages, ice and water wore away the soft rock in the middle. The harder rock at the top held firm. From the parking lot above the campground, allow 15 to 30 minutes for the somewhat steep climb to the hole, and 1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes for the full round trip.

See farmed salmon up close at Norsk Havbrukssenter, a center devoted to fish farming in Toft. Like Torghatten, it is on the other side of the Brønnøysund bridge. A walkway connects the shore to the fish farm. Using underwater cameras, the guide shows how salmon grow from eggs to adults. You then watch the fish being fed.

visits.text: Edvard Grieg’s villa is under restoration until summer 2027, but the grounds of Troldhaugen remain open year-round. The Norwegian composer lived here from 1885 until his death in 1907. In 1891, he had a small cabin built beside Lake Nordåsvannet so he could compose away from visitors. Edvard and Nina Grieg’s tomb is carved into the rock face, overlooking the lake. From mid-May to mid-September, admission is charged Tuesday through Sunday. The 200-kroner ticket also includes admission to the KODE museums in the city center.

visits.text: Norwegians call it Trolltunga, the “troll’s tongue”: a blade of rock jutting out over a sheer drop, about 700 m above Lake Ringedalsvatnet. It dates from the last ice age, about 10,000 years ago. Meltwater froze in cracks in the gneiss, a very ancient rock, breaking off blocks that the glacier carried away. Trolltunga is the part that stayed in place. Fewer than 800 hikers came each year before 2010, compared with more than 80,000 in 2016. In summer, expect to wait in line for a photo on the rock.

activities.text: Set aside a full day for the Trolltunga hike. From the P2 parking lot at Skjeggedal, at an elevation of 415 m, the round-trip hike is 27 km and takes 8 to 12 hours. Adding up all the uphill sections, you will climb about 1,200 m. The P3 parking lot at Mågelitopp, at 860 m, reduces the round trip to 20 km and 7 to 10 hours. You can hike without a guide from June 1 to September 30, and only if you have mountain hiking experience. Start early: the Skjeggedal road is only open from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m.

visits.text: Ishavskatedralen, designed by architect Jan Inge Hovig, was inaugurated on November 19, 1965. Its 11 aluminum-clad concrete panels on each side of the roof create the triangular silhouette visible from both the bridge and the airport. Inside, don't miss Victor Sparre's glass mosaic (1972) on the east side—it depicts the hand of God radiating three beams of light. Midnight sun concerts are held here in summer: check the program before your visit.

Tromsø's waterfront stretches along the Skansen district, where the old wooden harbor warehouses date back in some cases to the 1830s. This was the base from which shipowners financed Arctic expeditions in the 19th century—Tromsø was known as the Gateway to the Arctic. Walk here in the evening: the low-angle light on the colorful facades is particularly beautiful.

The Polar Museum (Polarmuseet) is housed in an 1830 customs warehouse and opened in 1978 on the exact 50th anniversary of Roald Amundsen's last departure from Tromsø. Inside you'll encounter his authentic equipment, a reconstructed Svalbard trapper's hut, and the story of Henry Rudi—a hunter who killed 713 polar bears over 27 winters and was a national hero of his era. Arrive in the morning: the museum is small and fills up quickly in the afternoons.

The Arctic-Alpine Botanical Garden is the world's northernmost botanical garden, open since 1994 on the university campus, with free admission at all hours. Its 25 collections bring together Arctic and alpine plants from every continent, from Tibet to Patagonia. The Himalayan blue poppy (Meconopsis) is its signature plant. Note that it closes when covered in snow in winter.

The Arctic University Museum of Norway (Norges arktiske universitetsmuseum) brings together collections on Sami culture, Arctic wildlife, and High North geology. You'll find presentations on the lives of Sami reindeer herders and their seasonal migrations—a valuable counterpoint before entering the landscapes ahead. Allow 1 hour 15 minutes and grab a map at the entrance: signage is primarily in Norwegian.

The Skansen district contains Tromsø's best-preserved wooden houses, painted in white, yellow, and red according to local tradition. This was the old residential heart of the city, established in the late 18th century. Take a walking tour in the afternoon: the streets are quiet, the facades photogenic.

Tromsø Cathedral (Tromsø Domkirke), built in wood in 1861, is one of Norway's largest wooden cathedrals. It stands out with its understated neo-Gothic style against the waterfront architecture. If you're here on a Sunday morning, the service is open to visitors.

Bodø→Tromsø flight (around 1 hour). Tromsø: an island connected to the mainland by a one-kilometer bridge, surrounded by fjords and mountains 350 km north of the Arctic Circle. With 77,000 inhabitants, it's Norway's eighth largest city, nicknamed the “Paris of the North”—a nickname from the 19th century, when upper-class women had their dresses imported directly from Paris and nightlife was surprisingly lively for such a northern city. Start with the Arctic Cathedral (Ishavskatedralen), built in 1964–1965 by architect Jan Inge Hovig: its triangular silhouette symbolizes icebergs, the long darkness and the northern lights. The eastern stained glass window—140 m² of glass—is one of Europe's largest.

The Polar Museum (Polarmuseet) occupies a former customs warehouse dating from 1833, listed as a national heritage site since 2000. It traces whaling, sealing, and the great polar expeditions. Roald Amundsen—the first man to reach the South Pole in 1911—has an entire room devoted to him, as does Fridtjof Nansen. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

At the end of the day, stroll through Tromsø's old town: the colorful wooden houses from the 19th and 20th centuries are among the best preserved in Northern Norway. The wooden church in the center (Tromsø Domkirke, 1861) is Norway's only wooden Lutheran cathedral.

Start with the Fjellheisen cable car, in service since 1961. In four minutes, it takes you up to 420 meters on Mount Storsteinen. The panorama takes in the city on its island, the one-kilometer bridge, the fjords and mountains on the horizon. In winter, it's one of Tromsø's best spots to observe the auroras. In summer, it's the starting point for hikers heading to Tromsdalstinden (1,238 m).

Stop by Mack Brewery, founded in 1877 by Ludwig Markus Mack, son of a German immigrant. Mack long remained the world's northernmost brewery. Its historic pub, Ølhallen, open since 1928, is Tromsø's oldest brewery-bar. It's the perfect spot for an Arctic beer facing the old docks.
A detour through Polaria, the Arctic aquarium whose building evokes white concrete dominoes toppled by a wave. Inside, bearded seals, Arctic fish and an exhibition on phenomena of the Far North.

activities.text: The Fjellheisen cable car opened on February 22, 1961, and carries passengers in 4 minutes up to the Storsteinen plateau at 421 meters. From there, the view sweeps across the entire city on its island and the Lyngen Alps in the distance. In winter, this is one of Tromsø's best spots for northern lights. Book ahead in high season—the cabins hold only 28 people.

Head out on a boat excursion into the Kvaløysundet to observe white-tailed eagles—the fjords around Tromsø are home to one of Europe's densest populations. These birds, with wingspans that can exceed 2.4 meters, dive for fish at the surface. Operators offer 2-hour trips departing from the harbor; book ahead in high season.

In the dark season (September–March), a nighttime northern lights excursion from Tromsø is essential. Operators offer outings by minibus or boat to the surrounding fjords. Tromsø is one of Europe's best bases for this: the sky is statistically clear more often than in other places at comparable latitudes.

If you have a car, head out to the island of Kvaløya for wild fjords less than an hour away. Local hikers go there all year round. In the evening, prepare for your flight back to Stockholm the following day.

visits.text: Nidaros Cathedral (Nidarosdomen) is the world's northernmost Gothic cathedral. Construction began in 1070 on the tomb of Saint Olav - a Viking king who died at Stiklestad in 1030 and was canonised a year later. His silver shrine was melted down for coins at the 1537 Reformation and his remains buried in a secret location within the cathedral that no one has found since.

The Archbishop's Palace (Erkebispegården), right next to the cathedral, is Scandinavia's oldest secular building still standing. It houses the Norwegian crown jewels and an archaeological exhibition on medieval Trondheim.

Bakklandet is Trondheim's most photogenic quarter - its colourful wooden houses and cobbled streets date from the 1600s. In 1965, the city council wanted to demolish the district for a four-lane highway; activists reclaimed the empty houses in 1971 and painted the façades to save them. Cross the Old Bridge (Gamle Bybro, 1681) to reach it from the centre.

The wooden storehouses on stilts (Bryggen) lining the Nidelva are Trondheim's equivalent of Bergen's Bryggen - built partly into the river to allow boats to moor directly. The view from the Old Bridge is Trondheim's postcard shot.

Kristiansten Fortress (1681), built after the great fire that devastated Trondheim the same year, dominates the town from its hilltop. From here you have the best view of the Nidelva storehouses, the cathedral and the distant fjord. Entry is free.

Ringve Museum, the national museum of music, occupies an 18th-century manor surrounded by botanical gardens. The collection of historical instruments is displayed in the original rooms - guides play live during the tour.

Munkholmen island, accessible in 10 minutes by boat from the harbour, has served variously as an execution site, Benedictine monastery (11th century), prison (17th century) and fortress. In summer, Trondheim locals swim from the beach there.

Trøndelag Folk Museum (Trøndelag Folkemuseum) at Sverresborg brings together historic farms and buildings in an open-air setting on the hills above Trondheim. The medieval Sverresborg fortress stands prominently at the centre of the site.

Trampe, the world's only bicycle lift, has stood on the Brubakken slope in Bakklandet since 1993. You place your foot on the pedal platform, the mechanism pushes – and you ascend the steep hill effortlessly. Available during the summer season.

activities.text: Wander through Bakklandet's lanes – the district's crooked houses are home to a concentration of independent cafés, bookshops and craft boutiques. Don't miss Trampe, the world's first bicycle lift, installed on the Brubakken slope in 1993.

The Ladestien coastal path follows 14 km of coastline north of Trondheim with views over Trondheimsfjord. You can walk part of it from Nedre Elvehavn - allow 2 to 3 hours for a one-way stretch to Lade and return by bus.

At the Sverresborg museum in Trondheim, follow the paths between the farms and historic buildings of Trøndelag. Observe the architecture of the houses, then climb to the remains of the medieval fortress to see the city and the fjord. This walk through the open-air museum offers a glimpse of the region's traditional ways of life.

visits.text: The Tysso I power plant, on the fjord in Tyssedal, houses Kraftmuseet, a museum of hydroelectric power and industry. From 1908 to 1989, it supplied electricity to Odda’s factories. Water flowed down through pipes from 400 m above, creating very high pressure. It was the first power plant of this type in Northern Europe. Don’t miss the control room with its marble panels. The museum is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. from May 23 to August 30; admission is 125 NOK.

activities.text: Next, climb to Lilletopp, at the top of the penstock, the large pipes that carried water down from the mountain to the power plant. The trail, equipped with steps and handrails, is 3.3 km round-trip with about 250 m of elevation gain: allow 40 to 50 minutes to reach the top. Up there, you can see where the old water tunnels ended, with views across to the Sørfjord, an arm of the Hardangerfjord, and Folgefonna Glacier. Park at P1, near the Tyssohallen sports hall: your museum ticket includes 3 hours of free parking there.

days_plan.itin_title: Southern Hardanger in 3 Days: Trolltunga, Folgefonna, Rosendal

visits.text: Ulefos Hovedgaard is a large manor house completed in 1807 in the Empire style, the neoclassical style of Napoleon’s era. It served as the summer residence of the Aall family, who lived there until 2007. The village is known for its ironworks, Ulefos Jernværk, founded in 1657. The reception rooms, including a “king’s room,” were designed to impress guests. Finish in the garden, which is very beautiful in summer. The manor is open in summer from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., except Mondays: visit right after the cruise.

activities.text: The most beautiful way to see the Telemark Canal is from the deck of an old boat. This 105 km canal connects Skien to Dalen through 18 locks. Completed in 1892, it was considered in Europe to be the “eighth wonder of the world” at the time. The Ulefoss–Lunde–Ulefoss half-day trip begins with a bus ride to Lunde Lock. You then travel back down aboard the M/S Victoria or M/S Henrik Ibsen, passing through the Vrangfoss locks to Ulefoss. Meet at the Ulefoss locks bus stop at 12:05 p.m.; the boat arrives in Ulefoss at 3:20 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Telemark in 4 Days: Rjukan, Heddal, and the Telemark Canal

visits.text: From the summit of Ulriken, at 643 m, you can take in all of Bergen at a glance. It is the highest of the seven mountains surrounding the city. The cable car even includes this elevation in its name: Ulriken643. At the summit, you will find a television tower, a restaurant, and a café. Strong hikers can walk to Fløyen along the Vidden route, a hike of about 5 hours across the mountains. From October through December, the cable car runs until 11 p.m. Thursday through Saturday: the nighttime view is worth the trip.

activities.text: Each cabin of the Ulriken643 cable car, upgraded in October 2021, holds fifty people. The ride to the summit takes about five minutes. To reach the lower station, take line 2 of Bybanen, Bergen’s light rail, to the Haukeland sjukehus stop, in front of Haukeland Hospital. Then walk uphill for 5 to 10 minutes along a steep street that can be icy in winter. From April through fall, a shuttle, Ulriksbussen, also leaves from the city center near the tourist information office.

days_plan.itin_title: Bergen in 2 Days: Bryggen, Fløyen, Ulriken, and Grieg

visits.text: Steinsdalsfossen waterfall, 2 km from Norheimsund, is one of Norway's most visited for a simple reason: you can walk behind it and stay dry. A paved path follows the riverbank, climbs behind the 46-metre curtain of water and comes out on the cliff side. Kaiser Wilhelm II came here every summer for 25 years - until 1914; snowmelt flow peaks in May-June. Plan a same-day round trip from Ulvik.

The Hardanger suspension bridge (Hardangerbrua), opened in 2013, spans Hardangerfjord for 1,380 metres - one of the world's longest suspension bridges. It replaced a ferry service that connected Bruravik and Brimnes for decades. Stop at one of the panoramic viewpoints to see it in its entirety from the shore.

Ulvik, a village of a few hundred inhabitants at the head of Ulvikafjord, is nicknamed 'Norway's orchard'. The slopes around the fjord are covered with thousands of apple, pear and cherry trees - English Cistercian monks introduced fruit cultivation here in the 13th century. In May, the blossoming orchards transform the village into an Impressionist painting. Stroll along the waterfront and fjord shore.

The Ulvik Fruit and Cider Route is the only one of its kind in Norway: three family farms welcome you for cider and apple juice tastings. Hardanger cider has been awarded Protected Geographical Indication status - Norway's equivalent of an AOC. In autumn, harvests are at their peak.

The trails above Ulvik offer views down over Ulvikafjord and Osafjord - two quiet arms of Hardangerfjord encircled by orchards and birch forests. Marked local trails start directly from the village. Pack hiking shoes: some sections are on a slope and can be slippery in wet weather.

Vøringsfossen waterfall, 20 km from Eidfjord, is Norway's most famous: 163 metres of free fall from the Hardangervidda plateau into the Måbødalen valley. In 1880, a hotel was built right on the edge - all the materials were carried up on horseback from Eidfjord. A 47-metre bridge opened in 2020, with 99 steps above the gorge, offers a dizzying view of the waterfall. For access by car from Ulvik, allow approximately 52 km and a 50-minute drive.

activities.text: Drive from Bergen to Ulvik via Norheimsund and Hardangerfjord: allow 2 hours 30 minutes. The scenic Alvikvegen road along the fjord is worth the detour - the road hugs the water a few metres up with constant views over the green waters of Hardangerfjord and the snow-capped peaks in the background.

Scenic loop from Ulvik to Eidfjord and back via RV7 - allow half a day. The section of road that descends through the hairpin tunnels of Måbødalen valley is spectacular: the transition from lunar plateau at 1,250 m to green valley to fjord happens in a few kilometres.

visits.text: The ferry crossing is worth the trip: Urnes Stave Church is the only church of its kind on the UNESCO World Heritage List, where it was inscribed in 1979. This type of church is supported by a framework of tall vertical posts. This one was built around 1130. Its north portal, carved around 1070 for an earlier church, was reused here. Its interlaced animals gave their name to the Urnes style, the last Viking decorative style. Open May 2–September 30, from 10:30 a.m. to 5:45 p.m., in groups of no more than 25: expect a wait.

activities.text: If the next tour group is full, wait your turn on the TRANQUIL trail. This poetry trail, opened in 2024, circles Urnes Church through the surrounding farmland and its apple orchards. Children can enjoy a playground, a nature trail, and a mock archaeological dig. At the neighboring Urnes Gard farm, a café sells local fruit, juices, and jams.

visits.text: In Kven, the language of the descendants of Finnish immigrants, Vadsø is called Vesisaari. Innvandrermonumentet, the immigrant monument, honors the families who came from Finland and northern Sweden in the 19th century to escape famine. Sculptor Ensio Seppänen depicted an old man with a spade, his daughter carrying a child, and, behind them, her husband, a Norwegian fisherman. The kings of Norway and Sweden and Finnish President Kekkonen attended the unveiling on June 18, 1977. Walk around it: the anchor at the back symbolizes these families putting down roots here.

Vadsø’s most evocative museum is a former merchant’s house: Esbensengården, the Esbensen estate. It is part of Vadsø museum, also called Ruija kvenmuseum, the Kven museum. Here you can see a 19th-century merchant’s warehouses and the comforts his family enjoyed. The museum also tells the story of the Kvens’ arrival and the town’s history of fishing, farming, and trade. The museum houses open seasonally or on request: check opening hours with the Varanger Museum before visiting.

Tuomainengården, the Tuomainen farm, shows how a Kven family lived in Vadsø. Around the courtyard stand the house, barn, stable, forge, bakehouse—the room containing the bread oven—and sauna. The buildings illustrate local construction methods. A café operates here regularly, near the old bread oven. Like Esbensengården, the farm opens seasonally or on request: ask the museum for dates.

In 1926, the airship Norge moored at Luftskipsmasta, the mooring mast on the island of Vadsøya, before flying over the North Pole. On board were Roald Amundsen and the Italian Umberto Nobile. Nobile returned here in 1928 with another airship, the Italia. This is the only mast of its kind on the European mainland. It stands in Vadsøya Cultural Park, 500 m from the center via a bridge. A flat 1.8 km trail passes the remains of a medieval fishing village and German bunkers.

Gray concrete and straight lines: Vadsø Church, Vadsø kirke, looks unlike the wooden churches elsewhere on this trip. It was consecrated on March 30, 1958, and designed by architect Magnus Poulsson. It replaces the previous church, burned by the retreating German army on the night of October 28–29, 1944. It can accommodate about 480 people. If the door is open, take a look inside.

visits.text: A work of art or a whim of nature? At Steinplassen, on the Valdresflye road, two boulders stacked one on top of the other form the installation Rock on Top of Another Rock (a rock on top of another rock). It is the work of artists Peter Fischli and David Weiss. The piece recalls cairns, the piles of stones hikers stack to mark a trail or a summit. Stop for ten minutes.

Flye 1389, a rest area with a café, takes its name from the elevation of the highest point on Valdresflye, the scenic route crossing this high plateau. In Norwegian, the word “flye” means a flat mountain plateau. The café, which opened in 2020, serves products from Valdres and Gudbrandsdal, such as waffles, cheese, and dried meat. In clear weather, the view stretches across the peaks of Jotunheimen, including Besshøe and Tjønnholstinden. Take your lunch break here.

days_plan.itin_title: Norway’s Mountains in 5 Days: Lillehammer and Jotunheimen

visits.text: Várjjat Sámi Musea, the Varanger Sámi museum, occupies a building in Varangerbotn dating from 1994 and inspired by traditional Sámi houses. Its main exhibition focuses on the coastal Sámi, who made their living from fishing, reindeer herding, and raising farm animals. It reaches back to the Stone Age. It also presents ancient Sámi beliefs. The museum maintains the Mortensnes site, your next stop: visit here first to better understand it. Near the museum, a shelter displays a map of Varangerhalvøya National Park.

visits.text: The most powerful place on the trip is a long wooden corridor: Steilneset minnested, the memorial to the Vardø witch trials. From 1600 to 1692, 91 people from Finnmark, both Norwegians and Sámi, were sentenced to death for witchcraft. Many were burned on this very spot. Swiss architect Peter Zumthor incorporated 91 small windows into the corridor. Each is lit by a light bulb and paired with a plaque recounting one victim’s trial. In the neighboring glass pavilion, Louise Bourgeois installed a chair with a flame rising from it, surrounded by mirrors. Free access, day and night.

Vardøhus festning, Vardø’s fortress, forms an eight-pointed star. It was built from 1734 to 1738 on the site of an earlier fort erected around 1300. It is described as the world’s northernmost fortress. When the sun returns after the polar night, the winter period when it does not rise, the fortress fires two cannon shots, and Vardø’s schoolchildren get the rest of the day off. Look for the Kongestokken, an oak log into which Norwegian kings have carved their names. Free admission from 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. in summer.

Finnmark’s oldest museum is Vardø museum, which opened in 1894 as a natural history museum. Today it occupies Gammelskolen, the town’s former school. It tells the story of trade with the Pomors, Russian merchants from the White Sea who came every summer to buy fish and sell wheat and timber. This trade helped Vardø gain town status in 1789. The museum also covers fishing, the witch trials, and the partisans, the resistance fighters of World War II. Check opening hours with Varanger Museum, which oversees it.

activities.text: Ask the tourist office for a map of the murals in Vardø, Norway’s easternmost town. In 2012, the Komafest festival invited artists from around the world, including Portugal’s Vhils and Belgium’s Roa, to paint dozens of buildings, many of them vacant. The town had lost about half its population between the 1960s and the 2000s. The name comes from the Norwegian word koma, meaning coma: the idea was to wake up sleeping houses. As you arrive, note the Vardø Tunnel, which descends to 88 m below sea level over its 2.9 km length.

visits.text: If you visit just one place on Vega, choose Vega verdensarvsenter, the World Heritage Center in Gardsøy. The archipelago has been UNESCO-listed since 2004 for a 1,500-year-old tradition. Residents build small shelters where eiders, wild sea ducks, nest each spring. Once the young have left, the down remaining in the nests is collected. Opened in 2019, the center takes 45 minutes to 2 hours to visit and offers free parking.

Small but packed with details, E-huset in Nes is a museum devoted to the eider, housed in a former store in this fishing hamlet. The original counter is still there, along with shelves filled with goods from days gone by. The museum tells the story of Vega’s residents as guardians of the migratory birds that nest on the island. Nes is about 16 km from the Igerøy dock. Call before you come: hours vary by season.

activities.text: Climb Vegatrappa, a stone staircase with more than a thousand steps, to the summit of Ravnfloget on Vega’s west coast. The walk covers 950 m with about 310 m of elevation gain and takes 30 to 60 minutes each way. At the top, views stretch across the archipelago and the island of Søla. Vega lies south of the Arctic Circle. Yet the atmosphere bends the sun’s rays, making it appear slightly higher than it actually is: this is refraction. Thanks to this effect, you can see the midnight sun in midsummer.

Sand beneath your feet at 65 degrees north latitude: Kjulstranda, on Vega’s southeast coast, is a sandy beach well suited to swimming. The shallow water is also good for playing and snorkeling. An open wooden shelter with a fire pit provides a place to picnic. The parking lot is small, so arrive early on days with good weather.

days_plan.itin_title: Helgeland Coast in 5 Days: Torghatten, Vega, and Svartisen

visits.text: Norwegians call him Sinnataggen, “the little hothead”: this furious toddler is one of the most popular statues in Vigeland Park (Vigelandsparken). Sculptor Gustav Vigeland designed the park’s 212 bronze and granite sculptures from the 1920s until his death in 1943. Monolitten, a stone column, stands over 14 m tall. Its 121 human figures were carved from a single block. The park is free and open day and night: come early in the morning to enjoy it in peace.

visits.text: With five chambers arranged like steps in a staircase, Vrangfoss is the largest lock station on the Telemark Canal. A lock is a chamber enclosed by gates: the water inside is raised or lowered to move a boat between different levels. Here, boats rise or descend 23 m. The name comes from the former waterfall, which was so “vrang,” meaning unruly, that logs floated down the river had trouble passing through it. Climb to the small yellow shelter by the upper chamber to watch the boats pass.

visits.text: Henningsvær, nicknamed the “Venice of the Lofoten,” spreads across several small islands connected by bridges—on Google Maps, you can clearly see the shape of the miniature archipelago. Park at the entrance and explore on foot: the streets are too narrow for cars. The harbor and its old converted fishing warehouses are listed as cultural heritage sites in Norway. Cod fishing remains the main activity—in February–March, the cod season transforms the quays into a scene of continuous work.

Henningsvær's soccer field is probably the most photographed in the world: built on a rocky islet between two arms of the sea, without stands—spectators bring their own chairs. The local club uses it for amateur matches, and the site also hosts concerts and festivals.

The KaviarFactory is one of the most unexpected cultural surprises in Northern Norway. Opened in 2013 in a former 1950s caviar factory converted into 500 m² of exhibition space, it presents internationally renowned artists—Ai Weiwei, Marina Abramovic, Yoko Ono have all exhibited here. A short walk away, Galleri Lofoten displays the largest collection of paintings from the “golden age of North Norwegian art” (1870–1930). Two museums of international standing in a village of 500 inhabitants.

activities.text: For a short but striking hike, climb Festvågtind (541 m). The ascent is difficult and short, but the 360° view over Henningsvær, the archipelago and the open sea is one of the most beautiful in the eastern Lofoten. Allow 2 hours 30 minutes round trip. Operators also offer sea kayaking among the islets around the village.

days_plan.itin_title: Scandinavia Road Trip: Stockholm to the Lofoten Islands

visits.text: The Abisko–Narvik road (85 km, 1 hour 15 minutes) crosses the Norwegian border at Riksgränsen and descends toward the fjords. In Narvik, begin at the War Museum (Narviksenteret). The Battle of Narvik from April 9 to June 8, 1940, lasted 62 days and cost 8,500 lives. It was at Narvik that Allied forces—British, French, Polish and Norwegian—won their very first land victory against Nazi Germany. The museum recounts these 62 days battle by battle, through photos, films and recorded eyewitness accounts. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

Narvik's harbor deserves a stroll: it's why the battle took place. Narvik was the export port for iron ore from Kiruna (Sweden) - an ice-free port year-round, connected to the Swedish mines by the Ofotbanen, the railway line built in 1902. Hitler needed this ore for his war industry: 90% of Swedish iron passed through Narvik in winter. The city still lives to the rhythm of this rail traffic.

activities.text: Take the cable car up Narvikfjellet for a panoramic view of the city, Ofotfjord and mountains from 656 meters. In summer under the midnight sun, the panorama is striking; in winter, it's one of the best vantage points for northern lights away from city lights.
